Projects prompts and responses into embedding spaces, fits separate Koopman-based predictive models for safe/unsafe regimes, and classifies using differential residual score comparing prediction errors. Incorporates prompt-response embedding dynamics to capture interaction patterns.
AI.result: Method evaluated across three safety benchmarks with three embedding models. Incorporating prompt embeddings yields consistent improvements, especially for interaction-dependent violations with causal decoders (e.g., Llama-3), while response-only violations benefit more from dense semantic embeddings.
AI.conclusion: Dynamical systems framework effectively addresses LLM safety classification in black-box settings. Approach enables analyzing AI systems with dynamical systems (reversing the typical paradigm of using AI to model dynamical systems), opening new research directions for AI safety analysis.

title: DeltaMomentum: A Key-Value based Anisotropic Momentum Update via Delta Rule
summary: Most modern optimizers form their momentum as an exponential moving average (EMA) of past gradients, forgetting every direction at one fixed rate. However, the inputs a deep network sees during training can be highly anisotropic, with a few directions queried frequently while most are seen rarely. Recent methods address this anisotropy by wrapping extra processing around this buffer, leaving the momentum update itself unchanged. We propose DeltaMomentum, which builds direction-awareness into the momentum update rule. The main observation is that the gradient of a linear layer splits into an input that acts as a key and an output-side error that acts as a value. Exploiting the key-value structure, DeltaMomentum updates the momentum buffer by the canonical delta rule, so each direction is forgotten at a rate set by how often it appears. We prove that it is a valid momentum, that it applies the input-side curvature correction without matrix inversion, and that it clears stale directions faster than EMA under both a fixed and a drifting optimum. It is a drop-in replacement for the momentum buffer of any optimizer, its coefficient transfers across widths under $μ$P, and its extra compute stays between $22.2\%$ and $25.0\%$ of a gated-MLP block's linear cost with no persistent memory. In FineWeb-Edu pretraining, AdamW with DeltaMomentum (DeltaAdamW) reaches AdamW's validation loss in up to $46.39 \pm 4.32\%$ fewer steps at 67M and $22.12 \pm 0.80\%$ at 370M over three seeds, and the gain persists at 1B on a Chinchilla-optimal budget. A Muon baseline tuned under the same protocol sits above DeltaAdamW at both language-model scales, and the gain holds for SGD, ResNet-18, and ViT-Tiny on CIFAR-10. Training-time diagnostics confirm the predicted mechanism, better gradient tracking and healthier input directions.

AI.tldr: DeltaMomentum is a novel momentum mechanism that uses direction-aware updates via the delta rule instead of exponential moving averages, providing better gradient tracking for anisotropic data distributions in deep learning.
AI.motivation: Standard momentum methods use exponential moving averages that forget all directions at the same fixed rate, which is inefficient for anisotropic training data where some directions appear frequently while others are rare. Recent approaches only wrap extra processing around existing momentum buffers without changing the core update rule.
AI.method: The authors propose DeltaMomentum, which exploits the key-value structure of gradients in linear layers: inputs act as keys and output-side errors act as values. This enables using the canonical delta rule for momentum updates, allowing each direction to be forgotten at a rate proportional to its frequency of appearance. The method is mathematically proven to be a valid momentum and applies input-side curvature correction without matrix inversion.
AI.result: DeltaMomentum demonstrates significant improvements: 22-46% fewer training steps to reach baseline validation loss in language model pretraining, with gains persisting up to 1B parameters. It outperforms Muon baselines, works for SGD, ResNet-18, and ViT-Tiny on CIFAR-10, adds minimal computational overhead (22.2-25% of a gated-MLP block's linear cost), has no persistent memory requirements, and transfers coefficients across widths under μP scaling.
AI.conclusion: DeltaMomentum provides a direction-aware momentum update rule that effectively addresses anisotropy in training data, offering faster convergence and better gradient tracking with minimal computational overhead, making it a practical drop-in replacement for existing momentum buffers across various architectures and tasks.

title: Scientific Data Skills: Enabling Agent-Ready Scientific Data Services at Scale
summary: Scientific data are increasingly used by AI agents, yet existing dataset representations provide limited support for autonomous discovery, interpretation, and invocation. This limitation stems from the fragmentation of scientific data across heterogeneous repositories and from dataset representations designed primarily for human use. To address this limitation, we introduce the Scientific Data Skill (SciDSK), an agent-ready representation that packages dataset-specific knowledge and operational guidance as a reusable agent skill. A SciDSK integrates dataset descriptions, scientific context, file organization, usage procedures, quality checks, and provenance information while retaining the underlying data in its original repository. We define a structured SciDSK specification and develop a systematic construction pipeline that grounds each SciDSK in authoritative dataset records and associated supporting materials. We further establish the Scientific Data Skill Bank, a unified platform that publishes SciDSK resources across six scientific disciplines and supports package access, persistent identification, and traceability to source datasets. We evaluate SciDSK through a retrieval benchmark for dataset discovery and controlled cases for dataset interpretation. The results show that SciDSK improves agent-driven dataset discovery and provides more precise and actionable support for dataset interpretation. These findings support the value of organizing dataset-specific knowledge in an agent-ready representation.

AI.tldr: SciDSK is an agent-ready representation that packages dataset-specific knowledge as reusable skills to enable AI agents to autonomously discover, interpret, and invoke scientific data.
AI.motivation: Existing dataset representations are inadequate for AI agents due to fragmentation across heterogeneous repositories and designs optimized for human use rather than autonomous agent operation.
AI.method: Developed a structured SciDSK specification and systematic construction pipeline that grounds skills in authoritative dataset records. Created Scientific Data Skill Bank platform publishing SciDSK resources across six disciplines with package access, persistent identification, and traceability features.
AI.result: Evaluation shows SciDSK improves agent-driven dataset discovery and provides more precise, actionable support for dataset interpretation compared to existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: Organizing dataset-specific knowledge in agent-ready representations like SciDSK adds significant value for enabling autonomous AI agents to work with scientific data effectively.

title: Beyond Multimodal Alignment: Certifying Physical Language through Response Substitution and Ordered Execution
summary: World models increasingly treat compact multimodal representations as interfaces between perception and physical interaction, yet existing probes do not establish whether different sensors carry the same executable meaning or whether that meaning survives a new action composition. We introduce an operational capability hierarchy and the Disjoint-Bridge Operator-Substitution Certificate (DBOSC), which asks whether independently trained modality compilers enter a frozen response chart interchangeably on evidence outside their training panels. On Cluster Haptic, audio and acceleration representations of the same unseen surface are 4.5x closer in response space than wrong-surface pairings, with the gap holding for all 19 held-out surfaces; unsealing withheld responses confirms that every branch predicts the physics better than the population chart. We then test ordered execution in a controlled elastoplastic system with complementary modality blind spots. At the pre-registered budget, the prerequisite refuses the stack because the frozen executor cannot advance even an exact chart coordinate through a held-out program. At a converged budget, the same rank-three chart executes those programs (oracle NMSE 0.18), fusion improves on both modalities, and 14 of 16 registered checks pass; the two failures arise because a diagonal restriction of the fused information matrix performs as well as the full one. Clearing the gate is a property of the executor, not the chart: an executor emitting whole programs instead of shared per-step dynamics is 38x worse than an entity-blind predictor on the same chart. A matching non-identifiability result explains why compression and fusion alone cannot determine an unseen composition law. These results separate attribute access, response substitution, fusion closure, and ordered execution into distinct, separately testable achievements.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DBOSC to test whether multimodal representations share executable meaning across different sensors and action compositions, showing that successful fusion requires more than just compression.
AI.motivation: Existing probes don't establish whether different sensors carry the same executable meaning or whether that meaning survives new action compositions, limiting our understanding of multimodal representation interoperability.
AI.method: Introduces an operational capability hierarchy and Disjoint-Bridge Operator-Substitution Certificate (DBOSC), which tests whether independently trained modality compilers can enter a frozen response chart interchangeably on evidence outside their training panels. Tests on Cluster Haptic datasets and controlled elastoplastic systems with complementary modality blind spots.
AI.result: On Cluster Haptic, audio and acceleration representations of the same unseen surface were 4.5x closer than wrong-surface pairings. The gap held for all 19 held-out surfaces. In controlled systems, at converged budget, rank-three charts executed held-out programs (oracle NMSE 0.18), fusion improved on both modalities, and 14 of 16 registered checks passed. A matching non-identifiability result explains why compression and fusion alone cannot determine unseen composition laws.
AI.conclusion: The work separates attribute access, response substitution, fusion closure, and ordered execution into distinct, separately testable achievements, showing that clearing the gate is a property of the executor, not the chart, and that compression and fusion alone cannot determine unseen composition laws.

title: Can Agent Memory Systems Track Evolving State?
summary: As LLM-based agents are deployed for longer and higher-stakes tasks, their memory systems continue to have crucial gaps. While existing memory benchmarks focus largely on recall-shaped tasks, we argue an effective memory system must track the evolving state of the world; as facts, constraints, and decisions are revised over a long interaction, answers must reflect the current state and not a superseded one. We define this capability as state tracking and instantiate it in StateMemBench, a benchmark of 234 multi-session scenarios spanning two conversation-length regimes. Its closed-pool grading scores whether an answer reflects the current state, the superseded state, or fails otherwise, separating state-tracking failures from other errors by construction. Our analysis shows that this task is challenging for existing memory systems, retrieval-augmented baselines, and long-context baselines. We then present StateMem, a state-first memory method that explicitly tracks supersession and relational dependencies, and show it improves current-state accuracy over the strongest same-backbone baseline by 1.8x (0.205 -> 0.363) on DeepSeek-V4-Flash and over the strongest memory system by 1.6x (0.149 -> 0.233) on Qwen-3.5-9B, while remaining competitive with the long-context baselines. Finally, we show the same state approach can be applied as a lightweight single-call wrapper over existing memory systems, lifting current-state accuracy by +32 to +67 points on StateMemBench across six memory and retrieval backends. A length- and cost-matched control attributes +15 to +32 of those points to state structure rather than added context.

AI.tldr: StateMemBench benchmark shows LLM memory systems struggle with tracking evolving world states; StateMem method improves accuracy 1.6-1.8x by explicitly tracking state changes and dependencies.
AI.motivation: Existing memory benchmarks focus on recall, but real-world tasks require tracking evolving states where facts, constraints, and decisions change over time. Current memory systems fail to distinguish current vs superseded states, creating crucial gaps for long-term, high-stakes LLM deployment.
AI.method: 1) Created StateMemBench benchmark with 234 multi-session scenarios across conversation-length regimes; 2) Designed closed-pool grading to separate state-tracking failures from other errors; 3) Proposed StateMem method that explicitly tracks supersession and relational dependencies; 4) Applied StateMem as lightweight wrapper over existing memory systems.
AI.result: StateMem improved current-state accuracy by 1.8x (0.205→0.363) on DeepSeek-V4-Flash and 1.6x (0.149→0.233) on Qwen-3.5-9B vs strongest baselines. As wrapper, lifted accuracy +32 to +67 points across six memory/retrieval backends. Control study attributed +15 to +32 points to state structure rather than added context.
AI.conclusion: State tracking is critical yet challenging capability for LLM memory systems. StateMem's explicit state-first approach effectively addresses this gap and can be integrated as lightweight enhancement to existing systems, significantly improving performance on evolving-state tasks.

title: Empirical Characterization of Learning Geometry in Hybrid Quantum Forecasting Models
summary: We characterize the learning dynamics of a compact hybrid quantum forecasting model through comparison with a structurally aligned classical baseline. Using stationary harmonic-mixture and nonstationary chirp benchmarks with controlled spectral complexity and data availability, we analyze empirical Neural Tangent Kernel dynamics through kernel-target alignment, kernel drift, spectral concentration, and training loss. The classical model exhibits stronger early target alignment, whereas the hybrid model generally develops a less concentrated kernel spectrum and smaller kernel drift. Despite these distinct optimization geometries, both architectures attain similar held-out performance across the evaluated regimes. Notably, the hybrid model uses 125 trainable parameters compared with 281 for the classical baseline and reaches its validation-selected checkpoint earlier in 15 of 18 frequency conditions. A Fourier-augmented classical baseline does not reproduce the observed training behavior, while a controlled re-uploading ablation shows that repeated encoding systematically modifies both optimization and kernel geometry. These results demonstrate that comparable generalization can emerge from substantially different learning trajectories and that individual NTK diagnostics do not provide monotonic predictors of validation convergence. Rather than claiming a general quantum advantage, the study identifies architecture-dependent learning behavior that is masked by endpoint accuracy alone.

AI.tldr: A comparative analysis shows hybrid quantum-classical models follow different learning trajectories than classical baselines but achieve similar generalization performance with fewer parameters and faster convergence, challenging simple NTK-based predictions.
AI.motivation: To understand how hybrid quantum forecasting models learn compared to classical counterparts, moving beyond just endpoint accuracy to examine optimization geometry and learning dynamics through Neural Tangent Kernel analysis.
AI.method: Compare a compact hybrid quantum model with structurally aligned classical baseline using stationary harmonic-mixture and nonstationary chirp benchmarks. Analyze NTK dynamics through kernel-target alignment, kernel drift, spectral concentration, and training loss. Include Fourier-augmented classical baseline and re-uploading ablation studies.
AI.result: Classical model shows stronger early target alignment but hybrid model develops less concentrated kernel spectrum and smaller kernel drift. Both achieve similar held-out performance, but hybrid uses only 125 vs 281 parameters and converges earlier in 15 of 18 frequency conditions. Fourier-augmented baseline doesn't reproduce training behavior, and re-uploading systematically modifies optimization geometry.
AI.conclusion: Comparable generalization emerges from substantially different learning trajectories, and individual NTK diagnostics are not monotonic predictors of validation convergence. The study identifies architecture-dependent learning behavior masked by endpoint accuracy, rather than claiming general quantum advantage.

title: Frequency-Aware Continual Learning for Smart Contract Vulnerability Detection with Large Language Models
summary: Smart contract vulnerability detection with Large Language Models (LLMs) faces three causally linked challenges. First, new vulnerability categories demand parameter-efficient adaptation, since full retraining is prohibitive for sequentially arriving tasks. Second, training per-task adapters on a shared backbone causes catastrophic forgetting of previously learned vulnerabilities. Third, the resulting multiplicity of adapters must be consolidated into a single model, since task identity is unknown at inference time. Each challenge arises directly from the solution to its predecessor, making an integrated framework essential. We propose a three-stage pipeline in which each stage addresses one challenge and feeds into the next. The adaptation stage uses Frequency-Aware Low-Rank Adaptation (FA-LoRA), which performs adaptation in the Fourier domain with per-frequency importance gates, requiring only 0.4% trainable parameters while outperforming standard LoRA and QLoRA. The continual learning stage applies Forget-Aware Replay (FAR), which uses these frequency gates to estimate per-sample forgetting risk via loss dynamics and prioritizes vulnerable knowledge for rehearsal, achieving an average Micro-F1 of 0.8022 across sequential tasks. The deployment stage employs Anchor-Protected Progressive Merging (APPM), which exploits the asymmetric generalization produced by FAR training to identify the strongest-generalizing adapter as an anchor and consolidates all adapters into a single model via anchor-protected weighted merging with frequency-domain gate competition. APPM achieves a Micro-F1 of 0.8085, within 2.7% of the independent per-task upper bound, at a merge cost of 156 ms and no additional runtime memory. Experiments on DIVE confirm the framework effectively addresses all three challenges for evolving blockchain ecosystems.

AI.tldr: A three-stage pipeline (FA-LoRA adaptation, FAR continual learning, APPM consolidation) addresses sequential vulnerability detection challenges in smart contracts using LLMs, achieving near-per-task performance with minimal parameters.
AI.motivation: Smart contract vulnerability detection with LLMs faces three causally linked challenges: 1) Need for parameter-efficient adaptation to new vulnerability categories without full retraining, 2) Catastrophic forgetting when training per-task adapters, and 3) Requirement to consolidate multiple adapters into a single model since task identity is unknown at inference time. Each challenge arises from solving the previous one, necessitating an integrated framework.
AI.method: Three-stage pipeline: 1) Adaptation stage using Frequency-Aware Low-Rank Adaptation (FA-LoRA) that performs adaptation in Fourier domain with per-frequency importance gates (0.4% trainable parameters). 2) Continual learning stage with Forget-Aware Replay (FAR) using frequency gates to estimate per-sample forgetting risk and prioritize vulnerable knowledge for rehearsal. 3) Deployment stage with Anchor-Protected Progressive Merging (APPM) identifying strongest-generalizing adapter as anchor and consolidating all adapters via anchor-protected weighted merging with frequency-domain gate competition.
AI.result: FA-LoRA outperforms standard LoRA and QLoRA; FAR achieves average Micro-F1 of 0.8022 across sequential tasks; APPM achieves Micro-F1 of 0.8085 (within 2.7% of independent per-task upper bound) with merge cost of 156 ms and no additional runtime memory. Experiments on DIVE dataset confirm effectiveness for evolving blockchain ecosystems.
AI.conclusion: The proposed integrated framework effectively addresses all three causally linked challenges for smart contract vulnerability detection with LLMs in evolving blockchain ecosystems, providing parameter-efficient adaptation, overcoming catastrophic forgetting, and enabling single-model deployment with near-optimal performance.

title: In Two Minds about Lifelong Learning: Exploring Hemispheric Redundancy and Specialisation in Neural Models
comment: 21 pages before references/appendix, 9 figures
summary: Persistent intelligent systems require the ability to learn continually, but current machine learning approaches face significant challenges in this area compared to biological learning systems. Machine learning algorithms typically trade off retention of previously learned information and adaptation to new or changing data patterns. When continual learning capabilities are absent, algorithms must undergo retraining using the entire data set, an approach that becomes impractical when original training data are unavailable due to storage constraints, financial or computational costs, or privacy restrictions. However, biological animals can learn continually, without experiencing catastrophic forgetting. This paper attempts to build a high-level framework for how animals learn and preserve knowledge by modelling neural components and states that are known to be related to memory consolidation. We focus on three concepts: experience replay, REM sleep, and bilaterality. We propose 4MAS (4 Module Awake/Sleep), a novel macroarchitecture demonstrating how machine learning models might benefit from asymmetric hemispheres, each with their own long- and short-term memory mechanisms, and how a period of sleep between incremental learning tasks might benefit memory consolidation. Finally, we present results showing that our architecture achieves competitive results on the Split-MNIST, Split-Fashion-MNIST and Split-CIFAR-100 datasets, with 98.3%, 84.9%, and 29.29% accuracy respectively.

AI.tldr: A biologically-inspired continual learning framework called 4MAS that uses asymmetric brain hemispheres, experience replay, and sleep phases to prevent catastrophic forgetting in machine learning.
AI.motivation: Current machine learning systems struggle with continual learning and suffer from catastrophic forgetting, requiring impractical retraining when new data arrives. Biological animals can learn continually without forgetting, suggesting nature has effective mechanisms that could inform machine learning architectures.
AI.method: The paper proposes 4MAS (4 Module Awake/Sleep), a macroarchitecture inspired by biological learning. It features asymmetric hemispheres with separate long- and short-term memory mechanisms, incorporates experience replay, models REM sleep, and includes a sleep phase between incremental learning tasks for memory consolidation.
AI.result: The architecture achieves competitive performance on continual learning benchmarks: 98.3% accuracy on Split-MNIST, 84.9% on Split-Fashion-MNIST, and 29.29% on Split-CIFAR-100 datasets.
AI.conclusion: Biological learning mechanisms like hemispheric asymmetry, experience replay, and sleep-based consolidation can be effectively modeled to create machine learning systems that learn continually without catastrophic forgetting, representing a promising direction for persistent intelligent systems.

title: Learning Hierarchical Skill Policies with Offline Quality-Diversity Reinforcement Learning
comment: IROS 2026
summary: Recent studies investigate how to leverage pre-collected datasets to improve the policy performance and sample efficiency of RL. One promising approach to achieve this goal is to employ a two-stage strategy: In the first stage, diverse skills are extracted as a low-level policy from a given dataset, and a high-level policy is trained to solve a specific task in the second stage. Typically, extraction of the low-level policy is performed based on unsupervised learning such as trajectory VAE. However, a limitation of this approach is that the quality of the low-level policy highly depends on the quality of the dataset. To address this issue, we introduce QDOS (Quality-Diversity Offline Skill learning), a unified pipeline for robust offline-to-online learning. Our approach incorporates an Advantage-Weighted Quality-Diversity pretraining objective, which weights the skill extraction and diversity objectives by the estimated advantage of each trajectory segment. This approach allows the model to extract diverse and high-value skills. By providing robust and task-relevant skill representations, QDOS significantly improves the quality of the embedded skill space used by the low-level policy. We further integrate this with a dual dataset reuse strategy, where offline data is used both for skill pretraining and for populating the online replay buffer via pseudo-labeling. Experiments demonstrate that QDOS significantly outperforms strong baselines in structured manipulation tasks and unstructured locomotion tasks, confirming its ability to accelerate exploration and improve final returns in challenging sparse-reward domains.

AI.tldr: QDOS is a two-stage offline-to-online RL method that extracts diverse, high-value skills from offline data using advantage-weighted quality-diversity pretraining, then uses these skills for efficient online policy learning.
AI.motivation: Existing offline-to-online RL methods that extract skills from datasets suffer from dependency on dataset quality - poor datasets lead to poor low-level policies. There's a need for more robust skill extraction that works well even with suboptimal offline data.
AI.method: 1) Advantage-Weighted Quality-Diversity pretraining objective weights skill extraction and diversity by the estimated advantage of each trajectory segment. 2) Dual dataset reuse strategy: offline data used both for skill pretraining and for populating online replay buffer via pseudo-labeling. 3) Two-stage pipeline: extract robust task-relevant skills from offline data, then train high-level policy for specific tasks online.
AI.result: QDOS significantly outperforms strong baselines in both structured manipulation tasks and unstructured locomotion tasks. It accelerates exploration and improves final returns in challenging sparse-reward domains by providing better skill representations.
AI.conclusion: QDOS provides a unified pipeline for robust offline-to-online learning that extracts diverse, high-value skills from offline data, overcoming dependency on dataset quality and enabling more efficient online policy learning in sparse-reward environments.

title: Continuous Adversarial MeanFlow Transfer
comment: Paper under review
summary: Training fast generators on new domains with limited data remains challenging for two reasons. First, adapting a pretrained diffusion or flow model to a new domain leaves its costly multi-step sampling unaddressed, and existing acceleration methods are tied to the source parameterization--$ε$, $x$, $v$, or $u$--leaving heterogeneous pretrained models with no common acceleration target. Second, while adversarial refinement is proven effective for few-step quality, it is formulated only for instantaneous-velocity flows, not for the finite-interval average velocities that MeanFlow (MF) models predict. We address both problems. We propose MeanFlow-Transfer, which maps heterogeneous source outputs into a shared velocity representation, uses it to initialize an MF generator from the source weights, and optimizes an MF objective on the target domain. This unifies adaptation and acceleration in a single training loop across a broad range of pretrained models. We then introduce Continuous Adversarial MeanFlow, a post-training stage that extends continuous adversarial flow models from instantaneous velocities to MF's finite-interval average velocities. CAMF contrasts changes in a learned potential between real and predicted interval endpoints, recovering fine detail that MF regression averages away, and reduces to the instantaneous criterion in the vanishing-interval limit. Adapting four ImageNet-based source models--DiT ($ε$), SiT ($v$), JiT ($x$), iMF ($u$)--to five target domains, MF-T with CAMF matches or exceeds the fine-tuned teacher in FID and FDD at up to $125\times$ fewer Neural Function Evaluations (NFEs), while CAMF improves MF-T's few-step FID by $29\%$ on average.

AI.tldr: MeanFlow-Transfer (MF-T) unifies model adaptation and acceleration into single training, with Continuous Adversarial MeanFlow (CAMF) improving few-step quality for diverse pretrained diffusion models.
AI.motivation: Two key challenges in training fast generators on new domains with limited data: 1) Existing acceleration methods are tied to specific source parameterizations (ε, x, v, or u), making heterogeneous pretrained models incompatible; 2) Adversarial refinement only works for instantaneous-velocity flows, not for MeanFlow's finite-interval average velocities.
AI.method: Proposed MeanFlow-Transfer maps heterogeneous source outputs into shared velocity representation, initializes MF generator from source weights, and optimizes MF objective on target domain. Continuous Adversarial MeanFlow extends adversarial refinement to MF's finite-interval velocities by contrasting potential changes between real and predicted interval endpoints.
AI.result: Adapting four ImageNet-based models (DiT, SiT, JiT, iMF) to five target domains, MF-T with CAMF matches/exceeds fine-tuned teacher in FID/FDD with up to 125× fewer NFEs. CAMF improves MF-T's few-step FID by 29% on average.
AI.conclusion: The approach successfully unifies adaptation and acceleration across diverse pretrained models while addressing the limitation of adversarial refinement for finite-interval velocities, achieving significant efficiency gains without quality loss.

title: Rethinking the Evaluation and Optimization of LLM-Based Social Simulation
summary: LLM-based social simulation is a promising complement to traditional methods such as surveys and behavioral experiments. A core question is how to evaluate the fidelity of LLM-simulated human behavior and optimize LLMs toward it. Prevailing practice evaluates by accuracy, checking whether the model selects the single response observed from a human, and trains the LLM to reproduce this hard label. However, human behavior is inherently subjective: the same person in the same situation may reasonably act differently, so an observed response is only one draw from an underlying response distribution, rendering accuracy-based evaluation unreliable and hard-label training misleading. To address these problems, we first introduce the subjectivity coefficient, an entropy-based quantity distinguishing objective tasks such as coding from subjective ones such as social simulation, and use it to systematically analyze how accuracy-based evaluation and hard-label training fail as subjectivity grows. Based on the subjectivity coefficient, we propose Subjectivity-Adaptive soft-Label Training (SALT): it pools observed outputs from semantically nearby inputs into soft distributional labels, with an aggregation radius adapted to the estimated subjectivity of each input; in the near-objective limit the neighborhood shrinks, so SALT naturally falls back to standard single-label training. Moreover, since existing datasets record only single observed responses and cannot support distributional evaluation, we construct SUBJSIM, a benchmark of 19,300 contexts covering 193 annotators and 100 subjective questions. Since real-world data typically provide only a single observation per input, our experiments train models from single observed outputs while evaluating them against the full response distributions, verifying feasibility in realistic settings. Results on SUBJSIM demonstrate the advantages of our method.

AI.tldr: Proposes Subjectivity-Adaptive soft-Label Training (SALT) and subjectivity coefficient to address limitations of accuracy-based evaluation and hard-label training for LLM-based social simulation, introducing SUBJSIM benchmark with distributional human response data.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based social simulation evaluation relies on accuracy metrics and hard-label training, which fails to account for inherent human subjectivity where multiple reasonable responses exist for the same situation.
AI.method: Introduces subjectivity coefficient (entropy-based measure) to distinguish objective vs subjective tasks; proposes SALT that pools observed outputs from semantically nearby inputs into soft distributional labels with aggregation radius adapted to each input's subjectivity.
AI.result: Created SUBJSIM benchmark with 19,300 contexts, 193 annotators, and 100 subjective questions; demonstrated advantages of SALT over traditional hard-label training when evaluating against full response distributions.
AI.conclusion: SALT provides better framework for LLM-based social simulation by accounting for human subjectivity, moving beyond single-label training toward distributional understanding of human behavior.

title: DraftFM: A FoundationModel for Day-Zero Drafting in Magic: The Gathering
comment: 28 pages, 6 figures, 13 tables. Sealed pre-registered forecast published ~36h before release; scoring note to follow. Also on SSRN (7257098). Code: https://github.com/brianward92/mtga Sealed forecast: https://github.com/brianward92/draftfm (tag draftfm-v1.0) Weights: https://huggingface.co/brianward92/draftfm Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/brianward92/draftfm-frozen-eval
summary: Drafting a new Magic: The Gathering expansion begins before any pick from it has been observed: the complete card list is public, but the draft logs that supervised pick models train on do not yet exist. We study this day-zero regime directly. DraftFM is a discrete-choice policy that scores exactly the cards available in the current pack, conditioned on the drafted pool and the state of the draft. Every card enters as a frozen 775-dimensional function of its public card record, structured features and a fixed text embedding, with no card identities, set identities, or usage statistics anywhere in the model, so an unseen card is scored by the same machinery as a familiar one. A 1.6-million-parameter network fitted on 149 million human picks from 29 expansions predicts held-out picks in three expansions withheld in their entirety, reaching 50.8%, 60.4%, and 56.7% top-1 agreement, where uniform chance at the opening pick is about 7%. Refitted on all 32 observed expansions, the same architecture produced a card ranking for the then-unreleased set The Hobbit, sealed with its complete cryptographic provenance and published roughly 36 hours before the set became draftable on MTG Arena. The sealed ranking agrees with six independent expert reviewers roughly as much as those reviewers agree with one another. Evaluation against realized outcomes is committed to a follow-on note, whatever it shows.

AI.tldr: A zero-shot draft pick prediction model for Magic: The Gathering that works without needing draft logs for new expansions, using card features rather than card identities.
AI.motivation: To solve the day-zero problem in Magic: The Gathering drafting where new expansions need to be drafted before any pick data exists, requiring models that can handle unseen cards without usage statistics.
AI.method: DraftFM: a discrete-choice policy using 775-dimensional card embeddings from public card records, structured features, and text embeddings. No card/set identities or usage statistics. Trained on 149M human picks from 29 expansions.
AI.result: Achieved 50.8-60.4% top-1 agreement on three withheld expansions vs 7% uniform chance. Successfully predicted picks for unreleased Hobbit set, with rankings agreeing with expert reviewers as much as they agree among themselves.
AI.conclusion: Zero-shot draft pick prediction is possible without card identities or usage statistics, enabling day-zero draft recommendations for new Magic expansions.

title: Beyond Memory Majority: Latent-Source Reasoning for Multi-Agent Memory Arbitration
summary: Long-term multi-agent systems continuously accumulate the memories produced by different agents. Existing memory methods typically treat retrieved memories as independent evidence and combine them through voting or weighting. However, this independence assumption often fails in multi-agent settings: memories written by different agents may inherit the same upstream source or shared bias, causing correlated evidence to be repeatedly counted and creating a false majority. We term this failure mode \textit{Memory Correlation Bias}. To address the issue, we propose the \textbf{C}orrelation-\textbf{A}ware \textbf{M}emory \textbf{A}rbitration (CAMA) framework that jointly decouples retrieved memories and recovers missing independent evidence. We model the retrieved memories as query-conditioned evidence groups and combine neural dependency inference with provenance-based symbolic priors to estimate the effective number of independent evidence sources, thereby preventing correlated memories from forming a false majority. Since critical independent evidence may be absent from the initial retrieval set, \textsc{CAMA} further learns a sequential recovery policy that actively retrieves alternative evidence or traces upstream sources before making the final decision, aiming to recover sufficient independent evidence for reliable arbitration while minimizing retrieval cost. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of our method over the state-of-the-art baseline methods, suppressing false majorities induced by correlated memories.

AI.tldr: CAMA framework addresses memory correlation bias in multi-agent systems by jointly decoupling correlated memories and recovering missing independent evidence through dependency inference and active retrieval.
AI.motivation: Existing memory methods assume retrieved memories are independent, but in multi-agent systems, memories from different agents may share common upstream sources or biases, causing correlated evidence to be repeatedly counted and creating false majorities. This memory correlation bias problem needs to be addressed.
AI.method: Proposes Correlation-Aware Memory Arbitration (CAMA) framework that models retrieved memories as query-conditioned evidence groups, combining neural dependency inference with provenance-based symbolic priors to estimate effective independent evidence sources. Also includes a sequential recovery policy that actively retrieves alternative evidence or traces upstream sources to recover sufficient independent evidence while minimizing retrieval cost.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate superiority over state-of-the-art baselines, effectively suppressing false majorities induced by correlated memories.
AI.conclusion: CAMA successfully addresses memory correlation bias in multi-agent systems by jointly handling correlated memory decoupling and missing evidence recovery, improving reliability of memory-based decision making.

title: A Two-Stage Time-Aware Transformer for Short-Horizon AECOPD Risk Prediction
comment: 7 pages. Accepted for publication in IEEE Systems, Man, and Cybernetics Letters
summary: Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (AECOPD) can worsen rapidly, making timely prediction a clinical priority. Most existing machine learning approaches rely on episodically collected clinical variables, introducing delays that limit their practical utility in home monitoring settings. Home ventilators offer a lower-latency alternative, producing a near-continuous record of respiratory status during daily use. However existing ventilator-based approaches either compress the waveform into handcrafted features or focus primarily on binary risk classification, leaving the timing of an impending event unresolved. In this paper, we present a two-stage framework that operates directly on raw pressure and flow waveforms from the most recent seven days of home ventilator use. The first-stage classification model identifies patients at high risk of a severe exacerbation. The second-stage regression model then estimates how many days remain before the event occurs. Our experimental results demonstrate that the two-stage model outperforms traditional baseline models on both risk classification and time-to-event estimation, with our selected Stage 1 classifier achieving F1 = 0.91 and our Stage 2 regression model achieving RMSE = 1.00 days and R^2 = 0.76, giving clinicians both an early warning and actionable lead time before a severe exacerbation occurs.

AI.tldr: A two-stage machine learning framework using raw ventilator waveforms to predict severe COPD exacerbations, providing both risk classification and time-to-event estimation.
AI.motivation: Acute COPD exacerbations (AECOPD) worsen rapidly, requiring timely prediction. Existing approaches use episodically collected clinical variables with delays, limiting home monitoring utility. While home ventilators provide near-continuous respiratory data, current methods either use handcrafted features or only binary classification without timing information.
AI.method: A two-stage framework using raw pressure and flow waveforms from the last 7 days of home ventilator use. Stage 1: classification model identifies patients at high risk of severe exacerbation. Stage 2: regression model estimates days remaining before the event occurs.
AI.result: The two-stage model outperforms traditional baselines on both risk classification and time-to-event estimation. Stage 1 classifier achieved F1 = 0.91. Stage 2 regression achieved RMSE = 1.00 days and R² = 0.76, providing both early warning and actionable lead time before severe exacerbation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully leverages raw ventilator waveforms to provide clinically useful predictions of COPD exacerbations, offering both risk assessment and precise timing estimates, which represents an improvement over existing methods for home monitoring applications.

title: SafeBranch: Branch-Pair Safety Alignment for Embodied Agents
comment: 25 pages, 12 figures
summary: Vision-language-model-based embodied agents can complete instructed tasks but often violate safety constraints in the process, a problem recently framed as interactive safety. Training such agents to act safely is difficult, since safety and task success are distinct objectives, and safety arises only at a small number of safety-critical steps within a trajectory. Standard supervision is insufficient: imitating safe trajectories teaches behavior without explaining why it is safe, and contrasting arbitrary safe and unsafe trajectories mixes the safety signal with unrelated differences. We propose SafeBranch, a framework that aligns an embodied actor on safety through branch pairs constructed from the actor's own unsafe rollouts via environment rollback. SafeBranch rolls each unsafe rollout back to the safety-critical step that caused the violation, queries the actor for a safe alternative, and pairs the original action with the alternative so that the two branches differ only at that step. The trained actor acts safely at deployment with no critic in the loop. On IS-Bench, SafetyALFRED, and out-of-distribution variants with unseen tasks and objects, it handles safety reliably without sacrificing task success, achieving roughly ten times more safe successes than the untrained baseline on the unseen-object variant.

AI.tldr: SafeBranch is a framework that trains embodied AI agents to act safely by using branch pairs constructed from unsafe rollouts via environment rollback, aligning the actor on safety without sacrificing task performance.
AI.motivation: Current vision-language-model-based embodied agents often violate safety constraints while completing tasks (interactive safety problem). Training these agents to act safely is challenging because safety and task success are distinct objectives, and safety only arises at a few critical steps. Standard supervision methods (imitation or contrasting trajectories) are insufficient as they don't isolate the safety signal or explain why actions are safe.
AI.method: SafeBranch constructs branch pairs from the actor's own unsafe rollouts via environment rollback. It rolls back each unsafe rollout to the safety-critical step that caused the violation, queries the actor for a safe alternative action, and pairs the original unsafe action with the alternative safe action. This creates branch pairs that differ only at the critical safety step, isolating the safety signal from other trajectory differences.
AI.result: On IS-Bench, SafetyALFRED, and out-of-distribution variants with unseen tasks and objects, SafeBranch handles safety reliably without sacrificing task success. It achieves roughly ten times more safe successes than the untrained baseline on the unseen-object variant. The trained actor acts safely at deployment without needing a critic in the loop.
AI.conclusion: SafeBranch effectively addresses the interactive safety problem in embodied agents by providing targeted safety training through carefully constructed branch pairs that isolate safety-critical decisions. This approach enables agents to learn why actions are safe rather than just imitating safe behavior, resulting in reliable safety performance even in novel situations.

title: Kähler landscapes for complex neural network descents and guarantees including a search and destroy of the Calabi-Yau manifold
comment: First version
summary: We study landscapes for complex-parameterized networks. Our approach is motivated with an information-theoretic manifold perspective of the parameter and via classical optimization guarantees although of complex geometric variety such as through Dolbeault asymptotics. The descent path admits a Kähler information metric under a cross-entropy via the Wirtinger Hessian on the log-likelihood potential. We restrict attention to a descent update rule with natural gradient descent via a differentiated loss scaled by the inverse metric, so the descent path remains in the holomorphic tangent bundle. We emphasize Calabi-Yau information manifolds which profane theoretical guarantees via an ill-curvature-conditioned landscape. Under a Calabi-Yau metric, specifically in a non-compact setting with a global potential so defined geometrically rather than invoking the topological requirements of the Calabi conjecture, a wedged nowhere-vanishing holomorphic form is the top exterior product of the Kähler form up to constants, yielding a constant determinant condition. Under a fixed determinant, a metric almost low rank up to an eigenvalue tolerance implies a blow-up effect. Moreover, it has been discovered that negative curvature subverts the loss landscape, specifically sectional curvature, so we expand on this and draw interconnections to negative-definite Ricci curvature. Our arguments primarily exist in a geometric analytic modality, although we establish roots in deep learning theory such as through asymptotics at initialization and connections through failure modes of neural network guarantees under vanishing and negative Ricci curvature.

AI.tldr: Complex neural network landscapes studied via information geometry, showing negative curvature subverts learning and Calabi-Yau metrics create ill-conditioned landscapes with blow-up effects.
AI.motivation: Motivated by information-theoretic manifold perspectives on network parameters and classical optimization guarantees, wanting to understand how complex geometric structures (like Kähler metrics and Calabi-Yau manifolds) affect neural network optimization landscapes and learning guarantees.
AI.method: Uses geometric analytic approach: information-theoretic manifold perspective, Kähler information metrics via Wirtinger Hessian on log-likelihood, natural gradient descent restricted to holomorphic tangent bundle, studies Calabi-Yau information manifolds with constant determinant conditions, analyzes curvature effects (negative sectional curvature and Ricci curvature).
AI.result: Reveals that Calabi-Yau metrics create ill-conditioned landscapes with blow-up effects when metric is almost low-rank, negative curvature (sectional and Ricci) subverts loss landscapes, connects geometric properties to failure modes of neural network guarantees under vanishing/negative Ricci curvature.
AI.conclusion: Complex geometric structures fundamentally affect neural network optimization landscapes, with Calabi-Yau information manifolds causing theoretical guarantee failures and negative curvature subverting learning, providing new geometric analytic understanding of deep learning failure modes.

title: GenMatch: An End-to-End Generative Matching Framework for Micro-View Order-Dispatching in Ride-Hailing
summary: Micro-View Order-Dispatching assigns available drivers to passenger orders within each dispatch batch and is critical to the service quality and operational efficiency of ride-hailing platforms. Mainstream industrial solutions follow a multi-stage paradigm of model prediction, value calculation, and dispatch matching. Although dispatch quality is determined by the final batch-level assignment, these stages optimize different intermediate objectives. This cross-stage objective inconsistency means that improving a single stage does not necessarily improve the overall dispatch result. We therefore formulate Micro-View Order-Dispatching as a generative matching problem and propose GenMatch, an end-to-end Generative Matching framework and the first such framework deployed in a real-world production environment. Applying generative modeling to this problem introduces three challenges. First, each dispatch batch forms a dynamic sparse bipartite graph, requiring efficient structured batch-level encoding. Second, replacing the hand-crafted value function requires learning unified business utility from heterogeneous feedback. Third, directly generating an assignment requires tracking the evolving matching state because each selected order-driver pair changes the remaining feasible candidates. GenMatch addresses these challenges with a Context-Aware Bipartite Encoder, a Business-Aware Utility Learner, and a State-Aware Pointer Decoder. Extensive offline evaluations and online A/B tests in five cities across DiDi's international ride-hailing markets show consistent improvements over competitive baselines, confirming the effectiveness and practicality of GenMatch for industrial order-dispatching.

AI.tldr: GenMatch is an end-to-end generative matching framework that solves order-driver dispatching as a generative problem, outperforming traditional multi-stage approaches by addressing objective inconsistency across prediction, value calculation, and matching stages.
AI.motivation: Traditional ride-hailing dispatching uses a multi-stage approach (model prediction → value calculation → dispatch matching) where each stage optimizes different intermediate objectives, creating cross-stage objective inconsistency. This means improving a single stage doesn't necessarily improve overall dispatch quality, which is determined by the final batch-level assignment.
AI.method: GenMatch formulates dispatching as a generative matching problem with three key components: 1) Context-Aware Bipartite Encoder for efficient structured batch-level encoding of dynamic sparse bipartite graphs, 2) Business-Aware Utility Learner to learn unified business utility from heterogeneous feedback instead of using hand-crafted value functions, and 3) State-Aware Pointer Decoder that tracks evolving matching states as each order-driver pair selection changes remaining feasible candidates.
AI.result: Extensive offline evaluations and online A/B tests across five cities in DiDi's international ride-hailing markets show consistent improvements over competitive baselines, confirming both effectiveness and practicality for industrial deployment.
AI.conclusion: GenMatch successfully addresses the limitations of traditional multi-stage dispatching by providing an end-to-end generative matching framework that directly optimizes final dispatch quality, making it the first such framework deployed in a real-world production environment for ride-hailing order-dispatching.

title: Unregularized Convergence of Single-Loop, Entropy-Regularized Natural Actor-Critic
summary: While entropy regularization is widely used to stabilize and accelerate Natural Policy Gradient methods, its ability to yield faster convergence rates for the unregularized objective remains underexplored. Existing analyses often rely on double-loop architectures and invoke a linear entropy penalty. To bridge the gap between theory and practice, we analyze a single-loop, entropy-regularized Natural Actor-Critic algorithm under compatible linear function approximation. By training an uncentered critic, our critic tracking can remain stable even as the training policy approaches determinism and the Fisher information matrix degenerates. We focus on two primary regimes for the optimization landscape: a Stochastic Regime, where we fuse coupled actor-critic updates into a joint Lyapunov recurrence, and a Deterministic Regime, where we pivot to a Policy Mirror Descent framework to circumvent the collapse of Euclidean geometry. By exploiting a positive Minimal Action Gap in the unregularized Markov decision process, we introduce an Exponential Translation mechanism that maps the regularized gap to the unregularized one up to an exponentially decaying tail. By tuning the fixed temperature, our algorithm achieves accelerated unregularized convergence rates, up to approximation-error terms: $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T_{total}^{-1})$ in the Stochastic Regime, and $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T_{total}^{-2/3})$ for the average iterate alongside $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T_{total}^{-1/3})$ for the last iterate in the Deterministic Regime. Here, $T_{total}$ denotes the total number of stochastic critic updates (or Monte Carlo rollouts). Furthermore, in the tabular setting, our positive-action-gap analysis yields a $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T_{total}^{-2/3})$ average-iterate rate, surpassing the $\mathcal{O}(T_{total}^{-1/2})$ worst-case statistical barrier that applies without a positive action margin.

AI.tldr: Entropy-regularized Natural Actor-Critic algorithm achieves accelerated unregularized convergence rates using a single-loop architecture with exponential translation mechanism, surpassing statistical barriers through exploitation of positive action gaps.
AI.motivation: While entropy regularization is widely used to stabilize Natural Policy Gradient methods, its ability to yield faster convergence rates for the unregularized objective remains underexplored. Existing analyses rely on double-loop architectures and linear entropy penalties, creating a gap between theory and practice.
AI.method: Analyze a single-loop, entropy-regularized Natural Actor-Critic algorithm under compatible linear function approximation. Use uncentered critic to maintain stability as policy approaches determinism. Employ two regimes: Stochastic Regime with coupled actor-critic updates and joint Lyapunov recurrence, and Deterministic Regime with Policy Mirror Descent framework. Introduce Exponential Translation mechanism mapping regularized gap to unregularized one.
AI.result: Achieves accelerated unregularized convergence rates: $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T_{total}^{-1})$ in Stochastic Regime, and $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T_{total}^{-2/3})$ for average iterate with $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T_{total}^{-1/3})$ for last iterate in Deterministic Regime. In tabular setting, positive-action-gap analysis yields $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T_{total}^{-2/3})$ average-iterate rate, surpassing the $\mathcal{O}(T_{total}^{-1/2})$ worst-case statistical barrier.
AI.conclusion: By exploiting positive Minimal Action Gap in unregularized MDP and using Exponential Translation mechanism, the entropy-regularized Natural Actor-Critic algorithm achieves theoretical acceleration over previous methods, bridging the gap between practical regularization techniques and theoretical convergence analysis.

title: TT-net: Quantum Inspired Tensor Network Denoising in Conditional GANs
summary: Developed as a workhorse for classical simulations of quantum algorithms and quantum many-body systems, Tensor Network methods have entered the scientific mainstream in quantum physics. Among various types of tensor networks, Tensor Trains (commonly know as Matrix Product States in the quantum computing community) have already found applications in machine learning. These methods often rely on a powerful linear algebra tool called the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD). Several conditional GAN architectures for image denoising incorporate SVD as a single-cut decomposition step applied to generator feature maps. In this work we introduce TT-Net, which replaces the per-channel SVD denoising block with a two-cut tensor-train decomposition capable of accessing cross-channel information directly, a capability absent from contemporary alternatives. In a controlled comparison differing only in this decomposition mechanism, TT-Net outperforms SVD-Net on PSNR and SSIM across all three noise types tested (Gaussian, motion blur, and salt-and-pepper), supporting the hypothesis that cross-channel access improves denoising quality. Training-dynamics analysis further shows that TT-Net's adversarial loss term consistently saturates to a stagnant state across all three noise types, more so than SVD-Net's, while reconstruction quality continues to improve regardless, raising an open question about the adversarial component's contribution that this work identifies but does not resolve. Furthermore, for Gaussian noise our method outperforms both the EigenGAN and the state of the art Pix2pix method which does not assume any linear algebra decompositions and does not retain any linear algebra information. Our manuscript shows how quantum inspired tools can be used as practical real world feature filters for deep learning applications.

AI.tldr: TT-Net replaces SVD denoising blocks with tensor-train decomposition for cross-channel information access, outperforming SVD-Net and other methods across multiple noise types in image denoising.
AI.motivation: Current tensor network methods in machine learning, particularly Tensor Trains/Matrix Product States, rely on SVD for denoising, but this approach lacks cross-channel information access which could improve denoising quality.
AI.method: TT-Net replaces the per-channel SVD denoising block with a two-cut tensor-train decomposition that can access cross-channel information directly, enabling better feature extraction across channels in GAN architectures for image denoising.
AI.result: TT-Net outperforms SVD-Net on PSNR and SSIM across Gaussian, motion blur, and salt-and-pepper noise types. It also beats EigenGAN and state-of-the-art Pix2pix for Gaussian noise. Analysis shows TT-Net's adversarial loss stagnates while reconstruction quality continues improving.
AI.conclusion: Cross-channel information access via tensor-train decomposition improves denoising quality, demonstrating quantum-inspired tools can serve as practical feature filters in deep learning, though the role of adversarial training components remains an open question.

title: Complementary, Not Cumulative: Interaction Effects in Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Navier-Stokes Vortex Shedding
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) embed governing partial differential equations directly into the training loss, offering a promising alternative to costly CFD solvers for unsteady flows. Yet the growing list of techniques proposed to improve PINN training is typically validated one at a time, leaving open whether these techniques actually compose. We study this question in depth on the DFG/Schafer-Turek unsteady cylinder wake benchmark. In isolation, nearly every technique performs no better than an untreated baseline. However, combining periodic (SIREN) activations with causal weighting unlocks a previously inaccessible regime, reconstructing velocity and pressure fields to within 4.1% average relative L2 error against an OpenFOAM reference solution. Adding further techniques instead causes catastrophic performance degradation, demonstrating that individually effective PINN interventions can interact nonlinearly and that more elaborate training recipes are not necessarily better.

AI.tldr: PINNs with periodic activations (SIREN) combined with causal weighting can achieve 4.1% error on unsteady cylinder wake benchmark, but adding more techniques degrades performance - individual improvements don't always compose well.
AI.motivation: Many techniques have been proposed to improve PINN training, but they're typically validated in isolation, leaving it unclear whether these techniques actually work together when combined.
AI.method: The study examines technique composition on the DFG/Schafer-Turek unsteady cylinder wake benchmark, testing PINN techniques individually and in combination against OpenFOAM reference solutions.
AI.result: Nearly all techniques performed no better than baseline when used alone. However, combining periodic (SIREN) activations with causal weighting achieved 4.1% average relative L2 error on velocity and pressure fields. Adding further techniques caused catastrophic performance degradation.
AI.conclusion: Individually effective PINN techniques can interact nonlinearly, and more elaborate training recipes are not necessarily better - the key is finding the right minimal combination that works synergistically rather than adding more techniques.

title: LLMs as Acquisition Policies for Finite-Pool Materials Optimization: A Controlled Study
summary: Discovering materials with desirable properties often requires searching large candidate spaces while experimental or computational evaluations remain costly. Active learning addresses this challenge by using previous observations to select which candidate to evaluate next, typically through probabilistic surrogate models. We investigate whether open-weight large language models (LLMs) can serve as standalone acquisition policies in this setting. We evaluate five LLMs across four retrospective finite-pool materials optimization tasks under different candidate-presentation strategies and compare them with random selection and conventional Gaussian-process methods. LLM policies generally reach the global optimum in fewer iterations than random selection, indicating that they provide a useful acquisition signal without task-specific training. Their performance relative to Gaussian-process methods is mixed: conventional acquisition performs better on most tasks, while LLMs match or outperform it in some settings. Performance varies substantially across tasks, models, initializations, and candidate presentations, with no LLM approach performing best across all tasks. Overall, open-weight LLMs show potential as acquisition policies for finite-pool materials search, although their reliability remains sensitive to the task and to how candidates and scientific context are presented.

AI.tldr: Open-weight LLMs can serve as acquisition policies for materials optimization, generally outperforming random selection but with mixed results compared to conventional Gaussian-process methods, showing potential but lacking consistency across tasks.
AI.motivation: Materials discovery requires searching large candidate spaces while evaluations are costly, creating a need for efficient active learning methods that can reduce the number of required evaluations.
AI.method: Evaluated five LLMs across four retrospective finite-pool materials optimization tasks with different candidate-presentation strategies, comparing them against random selection and conventional Gaussian-process acquisition methods.
AI.result: LLM policies generally reach the global optimum faster than random selection, showing they provide useful acquisition signals without task-specific training. Compared to Gaussian-process methods, results were mixed - conventional methods performed better on most tasks, but LLMs matched or outperformed them in some settings. Performance varied significantly across tasks, models, initializations, and candidate presentations.
AI.conclusion: Open-weight LLMs show potential as acquisition policies for finite-pool materials search, but their reliability remains sensitive to task characteristics and how candidates and scientific context are presented, with no single LLM approach performing best across all tasks.

title: Time-Uniform Self-Normalized Concentration for Discounted Least Squares: Limits and Corrections
summary: Self-normalized concentration inequalities are standard tools in bandit and reinforcement-learning analyses. A widely used weighted extension claims an analogous time-uniform guarantee for discounted least-squares estimators in non-stationary problems. A simple scalar Gaussian counterexample with a fixed parameter shows that the claimed bounded radius is crossed with probability one. For fixed discount and regularization parameters, we further show that, when $δ\leq1/2$ and $T/δ$ is sufficiently large, any deterministic anytime boundary valid uniformly over the stated conditionally sub-Gaussian model class must be at least of order $R\sqrt{\log(T/δ)}$ at some time by horizon $T$; for nondecreasing boundaries, this order is required at time $T$. We identify the proof error: different terminal times use different Gaussian mixing distributions, so the fixed-time mixtures do not form one supermartingale, and the stopping-time argument does not repair this failure. Finally, we show that the weighted inequality remains valid at each fixed deterministic time, give valid finite- and infinite-horizon corrections, and discuss consequences for downstream analyses.

AI.tldr: A weighted self-normalized concentration inequality for discounted least-squares estimators has a technical error - the claimed time-uniform guarantee fails, and any valid boundary must grow at order R√log(T/δ).
AI.motivation: The paper aims to correct a widely used weighted extension of self-normalized concentration inequalities in bandit/RL analyses. The claimed time-uniform guarantee for discounted least-squares estimators in non-stationary problems is problematic, and the authors identify the error and provide corrections.
AI.method: The authors provide a simple scalar Gaussian counterexample to show the claimed bounded radius is crossed with probability one. They analyze the theoretical limitations for fixed discount/regularization parameters, showing any valid deterministic anytime boundary must grow at order R√log(T/δ). They identify the proof error in the mixing distribution argument and provide fixed-time validity plus finite/infinite-horizon corrections.
AI.result: The claimed time-uniform inequality fails; any valid deterministic anytime boundary requires growth of order R√log(T/δ); the inequality remains valid at each fixed deterministic time; valid corrections are provided for finite- and infinite-horizon settings.
AI.conclusion: The widely used weighted self-normalized concentration inequality has a fundamental technical error in its time-uniform claim. The corrected analysis shows the necessity of logarithmic growth boundaries and provides proper corrections, with implications for downstream bandit and RL analyses that rely on such inequalities.

title: Towards general embodied intelligence: integrating large language models, knowledge bases, and reasoning capabilities to build the next generation of AI agents
summary: The convergence of large language models (LLMs), structured knowledge bases (KBs), and reasoning ability (RA) presents a promising trajectory toward general embodied intelligence (GEI). This paper reviews the evolution of LLM-centered intelligent systems, emphasising their integration with knowledge representation, logical reasoning, and physical embodiment. We analyse LLM architectures, pre-training methods, and inference mechanisms, along with their interaction with external knowledge sources and structured reasoning frameworks. Furthermore, we examine embodied intelligence (EI) paradigms wherein agents learn and act in physical environments. To synthesise these dimensions, we present a conceptual framework that illustrates the synergy among LLMs, KBs, RA, and embodiment, serving as a guiding model for perception, reasoning, and action rather than an implemented engineering architecture. To advance toward GEI, we identify five key challenges: efficient LLM deployment, closed-loop knowledge integration, hybrid symbolic-neural reasoning, perception-action grounding, and continual learning. This survey provides a comprehensive roadmap for developing adaptive, multimodal agents capable of operating in complex, dynamic settings.

AI.tldr: A survey paper proposing a conceptual framework integrating Large Language Models, knowledge bases, reasoning ability, and embodiment for achieving general embodied intelligence, identifying key challenges in the field.
AI.motivation: The convergence of LLMs, knowledge bases, and reasoning presents a promising path toward general embodied intelligence, but current research needs synthesis and a guiding framework to advance the field systematically.
AI.method: Comprehensive review of LLM-centered intelligent systems evolution, analysis of LLM architectures, pre-training methods, inference mechanisms, and examination of embodied intelligence paradigms. Presentation of a conceptual framework showing synergy between components.
AI.result: A conceptual framework illustrating synergy among LLMs, knowledge bases, reasoning ability, and embodiment that serves as a guiding model for perception, reasoning, and action. Identification of five key challenges for achieving GEI: efficient LLM deployment, closed-loop knowledge integration, hybrid symbolic-neural reasoning, perception-action grounding, and continual learning.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework and identified challenges provide a comprehensive roadmap for developing adaptive, multimodal agents capable of operating in complex, dynamic settings, advancing research toward general embodied intelligence.

title: DeltaML-Bench: Evaluating Machine Learning Agents on Real-World Research Repositories
comment: 18 pages, 3 figures, 12 tables. Code and benchmark: https://github.com/AlgorithmicResearchGroup/deltaml-bench-public
summary: Autonomous agents for machine learning experimentation must navigate heterogeneous repositories, repair training pipelines, and evaluate candidate improvements under realistic compute constraints. Existing benchmarks only partially capture these conditions. We introduce DeltaML-Bench, a benchmark comprising 48 tasks sourced from research papers that require agents to improve published baselines within imperfect, open-source repositories. We evaluate GPT-5 and Claude Sonnet 4 with a standard Modular agent and a search-based ARG scaffolding. In the 4 x 6h allocation, ARG raises GPT-5's per-run success rate from 9.4% to 33.9%; in the 2 x 12h allocation, GPT-5 ARG reaches 49.0%. Modular configurations exhibit specification gaming rates as high as 47.9%, while no gaming is observed in the evaluated ARG configurations. These results indicate that scaffolding design and integrity checks are important considerations when deploying agents for autonomous ML experimentation.

AI.tldr: DeltaML-Bench is a benchmark for evaluating autonomous ML experimentation agents with 48 tasks requiring improvement of published baselines in imperfect repositories. ARG scaffolding significantly improves GPT-5's success rates from 9.4% to 49.0%.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks don't fully capture the real-world challenges of autonomous ML experimentation, which involves navigating heterogeneous repositories, repairing training pipelines, and evaluating improvements under realistic compute constraints.
AI.method: Created DeltaML-Bench with 48 tasks sourced from research papers requiring agents to improve published baselines in imperfect open-source repositories. Evaluated GPT-5 and Claude Sonnet 4 with two approaches: standard Modular agent and search-based ARG scaffolding under different time allocations (4x6h and 2x12h).
AI.result: ARG scaffolding dramatically improved GPT-5's performance: from 9.4% to 33.9% success rate in 4x6h allocation, and up to 49.0% in 2x12h allocation. Modular configurations showed high specification gaming rates (up to 47.9%), while ARG configurations showed no gaming.
AI.conclusion: Scaffolding design and integrity checks are crucial for deploying autonomous ML experimentation agents, as ARG's structured approach significantly outperforms modular configurations while avoiding specification gaming.

title: ADAPT: Physics-Aware Diffusion-based World Models for Adaptive Predictive Transferable HVAC Control
summary: Buildings account for roughly one-third of global energy consumption and CO$_2$ emissions. Optimizing indoor climate systems plays a critical role for urban climate mitigation aligned with UN Sustainable Development Goals 11 and 13. However, indoor delayed thermodynamic responses and partial observability severely hinder existing methods, which are primarily limited by implicit thermal inertia, occupancy dynamic prediction, and cumulative prediction errors, especially for out-of-distribution environments. In practice, these challenges are further exacerbated by the high cost and privacy burden of dense indoor sensing, forcing operators to collect only limited data in a single operating regime while expecting controllers to generalize reliably across unseen seasons and climate regions. To address this problem, we propose ADAPT, a physics-aware conditional diffusion indoor environmental world model for HVAC control. The model predicts a short-horizon held-action thermal baseline to capture the latent thermal inertia of the buildings. The diffusion backbone utilizes the robustness of generative models, while a learnable multi-zone heat-balance regularizer constrains generated trajectories to satisfy transferable building thermodynamics without requiring known building geometry or manually calibrated thermal parameters. A credit assignment is then design for the downstream reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments on SemibuildingSim and Sinergym demonstrate that ADAPT reduces HVAC energy consumption by 7.3\% and occupant discomfort by 30.2\% compared with state-of-the-art baselines under IID control. Under OOD control scenarios spanning unseen seasons and climate regions, ADAPT maintains robust performance with only marginal degradation relative to its IID performance, substantially outperforming existing methods in transfer robustness.

AI.tldr: ADAPT is a physics-aware conditional diffusion model for HVAC control that improves energy efficiency and occupant comfort while maintaining robust performance across unseen seasons and climate regions.
AI.motivation: Buildings consume significant global energy (one-third) and produce CO2 emissions. Existing HVAC control methods struggle with indoor delayed thermodynamic responses, partial observability, thermal inertia, occupancy prediction, and cumulative errors, especially in out-of-distribution environments. Limited data collection due to cost/privacy constraints forces systems to generalize across unseen conditions.
AI.method: Proposes ADAPT: a physics-aware conditional diffusion indoor environmental world model for HVAC control. It predicts short-horizon thermal baselines to capture latent thermal inertia. The diffusion backbone leverages generative model robustness, while a learnable multi-zone heat-balance regularizer constrains trajectories to satisfy transferable building thermodynamics without requiring known geometry or calibrated parameters. Includes credit assignment for downstream reinforcement learning.
AI.result: ADAPT reduces HVAC energy consumption by 7.3% and occupant discomfort by 30.2% compared to state-of-the-art baselines under IID control. Under OOD scenarios (unseen seasons and climate regions), it maintains robust performance with minimal degradation, substantially outperforming existing methods in transfer robustness.
AI.conclusion: ADAPT effectively addresses the challenges of building energy optimization by combining physics-aware modeling with diffusion-based generative approaches, enabling reliable generalization across diverse environmental conditions without extensive sensor data or building-specific calibration.

title: Rationally Enriched Chebyshev Trunk Bases for DeepONet Surrogates of High Péclet Entrance Transport
comment: 39 pages, 9 figures
summary: This study demonstrates a rationally enriched Chebyshev (REC) trunk for deep operator network (DeepONet) surrogate models of singularly perturbed and high-Péclet transport problems whose solution profiles are characterized by thin localized boundary or wall layers. The REC trunk combines Chebyshev polynomial dictionary elements with rational dictionary elements constructed using the adaptive Antoulas-Anderson (AAA) algorithm. Over five independent training runs, the resulting REC-trunk DeepONet is evaluated against a vanilla DeepONet and a Chebyshev-trunk DeepONet whose prescribed dictionary consists only of Chebyshev polynomials across three problems whose singular perturbation parameters are diffusion-to-advection ratios: a singularly perturbed scalar boundary-value problem (BVP), the thermal entrance problem with a prescribed wall temperature, and the concentration entrance problem with an absorbing wall. Across the held-out test profiles, the REC-trunk DeepONet improves over the vanilla DeepONet and remains comparable to the Chebyshev-trunk DeepONet in predicting the scalar profile, with its clearest advantage over the Chebyshev-trunk DeepONet appearing when the perturbation parameter lies between $1.00\times10^{-4}$ and $1.78\times10^{-4}$, where it reduces the profile-error metrics by up to $19.5\,\%$ relative to the Chebyshev-trunk DeepONet. In predicting the wall-normal temperature and concentration profiles, the REC-trunk DeepONet reduces the profile-error metrics by up to $60.2\,\%$ and $32.2\,\%$ relative to the vanilla and Chebyshev-trunk DeepONets, respectively, while suppressing artificial near-wall oscillations as the Péclet or mass-transfer Péclet number ranges from $10^{2}$ to $10^{4}$.
