AI.tldr: REC-trunk DeepONet combines Chebyshev polynomials with rational functions to better capture boundary layers in singularly perturbed transport problems, reducing errors by up to 60% compared to vanilla DeepONet.
AI.motivation: Singularly perturbed and high-Péclet transport problems exhibit thin boundary/wall layers that are difficult for standard DeepONet architectures to capture accurately with polynomial basis functions alone.
AI.method: Developed a rationally enriched Chebyshev (REC) trunk for DeepONet that combines Chebyshev polynomial dictionary elements with rational dictionary elements constructed using the adaptive Antoulas-Anderson (AAA) algorithm.
AI.result: REC-trunk DeepONet improves over vanilla DeepONet and remains comparable to Chebyshev-trunk DeepONet on scalar BVPs, with up to 19.5% error reduction for specific perturbation parameters. For thermal/concentration problems, it reduces errors by up to 60.2% and 32.2% respectively, while suppressing near-wall oscillations across Péclet numbers from 10² to 10⁴.
AI.conclusion: Rational enrichment of Chebyshev trunks significantly improves DeepONet performance for singularly perturbed transport problems with boundary layers, offering better accuracy and oscillation suppression compared to polynomial-only approaches.

title: When Saying No Makes Better Videos: Designing Dual Gatekeeping for Pedagogically Grounded AI Content Creation
comment: 4 pages, 1 figure. Presented at the CHI 2026 Workshop on Understanding and Engaging Critical Resistance to AI in Education
summary: To prevent the adoption of aesthetically polished but pedagogically flawed AI content, we study a video authoring pipeline featuring two layers of structured refusal. The first layer empowers educators to iteratively reshape AI scripts based on multimedia learning theory, while the second employs automated metrics to flag violations in instructional coherence and narrative-visual synchronization. While neither layer is exhaustive, their synergy ensures that principled resistance--the act of deferring AI output until it meets rigorous standards--becomes a catalyst for higher quality. Evaluation combining a study with 23 educators across 3 topics and automated metrics across 7 topics drawn from established science and philosophy curricula shows that both layers independently improve the same instructional dimensions, suggesting that thoughtful resistance and generative AI are not opposites but partners.

AI.tldr: A video authoring system with two-layer structured refusal to improve AI-generated educational content quality by combining educator judgment with automated metrics.
AI.motivation: To prevent adoption of aesthetically polished but pedagogically flawed AI-generated educational content, which may look good but lack instructional effectiveness.
AI.method: A two-layer structured refusal pipeline: 1) Educator iterative reshaping of AI scripts based on multimedia learning theory, and 2) Automated metrics to flag violations in instructional coherence and narrative-visual synchronization.
AI.result: Evaluation with 23 educators across 3 topics and automated metrics across 7 topics showed both layers independently improve the same instructional dimensions. The synergy ensures principled resistance acts as a catalyst for higher quality.
AI.conclusion: Thoughtful resistance and generative AI are not opposites but partners - principled refusal of AI output until it meets rigorous standards enables higher quality educational content.

title: FleetSieve: Decision-Critical Profiling for SLO-Aware LLM Fleet Configuration
summary: Choosing tensor-parallel (TP) degrees and replica counts for an LLM serving fleet is difficult because performance is not monotonic in TP and the feasible choice can change with load. Exhaustive profiling resolves this uncertainty, but measures many configurations that do not affect the final resource allocation. We present FleetSieve, which selects measurements according to their expected effect on a resource-coupled, SLO-aware fleet decision. FleetSieve models capacity and tail latency jointly, compares conservative and optimistic allocations, and stops when their remaining decision gap is below a specified tolerance. On a fixed H100 measurement grid for a 31B-parameter open-weight model, FleetSieve reaches the oracle aggregate decision using 22,200 GPU-seconds, 6.9% less than uniform random profiling in the fixed comparison. Across 200 random reveal orders, its mean saving over random profiling is 5.4% (95% bootstrap CI: 3.5-7.2%). The fixed-comparison saving is 21.5% for Chat, while FleetSieve does not use the fewest GPU-seconds for Code. Joint capacity and tail modeling also avoids selecting a configuration whose 46.4-second completion p99 violates a 30-second SLO. In a 16-GPU allocation, an incorrect sparse-profile decision loses up to 1.93 requests/s and 12.4 percentage points of max-min fulfillment. Boundary repeats and BurstGPT measurements support the observed load-dependent tail-latency mechanism.

AI.tldr: FleetSieve is an intelligent profiling system for LLM serving fleets that selectively measures configurations based on their expected impact on resource allocation decisions, reducing profiling costs while maintaining optimal fleet planning.
AI.motivation: Choosing optimal tensor-parallel (TP) degrees and replica counts for LLM serving fleets is challenging due to non-monotonic performance in TP and load-dependent feasibility. Exhaustive profiling is costly as it measures many irrelevant configurations that don't affect final resource allocation.
AI.method: FleetSieve selects measurements based on their expected effect on resource-coupled, SLO-aware fleet decisions. It models capacity and tail latency jointly, compares conservative vs. optimistic allocations, and stops profiling when the remaining decision gap falls below a specified tolerance threshold.
AI.result: On an H100 measurement grid for a 31B-parameter model, FleetSieve achieves oracle aggregate decisions using 22,200 GPU-seconds (6.9% less than uniform random profiling). Mean saving across 200 random orders is 5.4% (CI: 3.5-7.2%). It saves 21.5% for Chat tasks and avoids selecting configurations that violate 30-second SLOs (detecting a 46.4-second p99 violation).
AI.conclusion: FleetSieve effectively reduces profiling costs for LLM serving fleet configuration while maintaining optimal resource allocation decisions, with particular benefits for tail-latency-sensitive applications and avoidance of SLO violations.

title: Causal Reasoning with Bipartite Graphical Causal Models
comment: Figure 2 was added w.r.t. to the published version at Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI) 2026
summary: Causal Bayesian networks (CBNs) and structural causal models (SCMs) are the dominant frameworks for graphical causal reasoning, but they cannot adequately represent all real-world causal systems. In particular, systems at equilibrium---where feedback mechanisms create cyclic causal dependencies---can exhibit causal semantics that are fundamentally incompatible with these frameworks: different interventions that enforce the same variable value may have different effects, rendering the standard ``perfect intervention'' do($X = x$) ambiguous. We propose bipartite graphical causal models (BGCMs), in which the structure of a system of equations is encoded by a bipartite graph with variable and equation nodes. In this framework, a hard intervention do($f_j : X_v = ξ_v$) specifies which equation is replaced, which variable is targeted, and at what value---resolving the ambiguity of the standard notion. We demonstrate, through a detailed case study of a physical system, that this representation naturally corresponds to distinct real-world interventions. We formulate a Markov property in terms of a new graphical separation criterion (B-separation) that exploits the functional determinism inherent in the equations, and we extend it to settings with non-random inputs. We show how this gives rise to a do-calculus for reasoning about domain invariances. BGCMs strictly generalize CBNs and SCMs while retaining the ability to perform graphical causal reasoning.

AI.tldr: BGCMs (bipartite graphical causal models) extend standard causal frameworks to handle equilibrium systems with feedback cycles by using bipartite graphs and specifying which equations are intervened upon, resolving ambiguities in standard perfect interventions.
AI.motivation: Standard causal frameworks (CBNs and SCMs) cannot adequately represent real-world systems at equilibrium where feedback mechanisms create cyclic causal dependencies. In such systems, different interventions that enforce the same variable value can have different effects, making standard "perfect intervention" do(X=x) ambiguous and inadequate.
AI.method: Proposes bipartite graphical causal models (BGCMs) where system structure is encoded by a bipartite graph with variable and equation nodes. Hard interventions specify which equation is replaced, which variable is targeted, and at what value. Introduces B-separation graphical criterion that exploits functional determinism in equations and extends it to non-random inputs.
AI.result: Demonstrates through a physical system case study that BGCM representation naturally corresponds to distinct real-world interventions. Formulates Markov property using B-separation and develops a do-calculus for reasoning about domain invariances.
AI.conclusion: BGCMs strictly generalize CBNs and SCMs while retaining graphical causal reasoning capabilities, providing a more comprehensive framework for representing causal systems with feedback cycles and equilibrium conditions.

title: SAGE-XGBoost: Spatially Augmented Graph Embeddings--Machine Learning Framework for Natural Hazards Susceptibility Mapping under Data Scarcity
summary: Natural hazard susceptibility mapping is often constrained by limited labeled data, reducing the generalizability of conventional machine learning and limiting the applicability of complex deep learning models. This study proposes SAGE (Spatially Augmented Graph Embeddings), a structurally informed feature-engineering framework that combines controlled noise-based data augmentation with neighborhood-based graph embeddings to improve prediction under data-scarce conditions. A K-nearest neighbor graph is constructed to derive local spatial statistics, which are reduced using principal component analysis and integrated with environmental covariates and spatial coordinates. The resulting features are used with XGBoost to develop the SAGE-XGBoost model. The framework was evaluated for landslide and wildfire susceptibility mapping. SAGE-XGBoost consistently outperformed conventional and spatially explicit machine learning models. Compared with Spatial XGBoost, it achieved an absolute improvement of above 33 percentage points across the two case studies. The model reached AUC values of approximately 0.97 for landslide susceptibility and 0.95 for wildfire susceptibility. Feature importance analysis confirmed the contribution of graph embeddings to prediction, while their integration improved spatial coherence and reduced local noise amplification. Overall, SAGE-XGBoost provides an efficient and transferable alternative to deep representation learning for environmental hazard assessment and other geospatial prediction tasks under limited supervision.

AI.tldr: SAGE-XGBoost combines spatial graph embeddings with XGBoost for natural hazard susceptibility mapping under data-scarce conditions, outperforming conventional methods by over 33 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Natural hazard susceptibility mapping faces limitations due to scarce labeled data, which reduces generalizability of conventional machine learning and limits applicability of complex deep learning models.
AI.method: SAGE framework combines controlled noise-based data augmentation with neighborhood-based graph embeddings. Constructs K-nearest neighbor graph to derive local spatial statistics, reduces them with PCA, integrates with environmental covariates and spatial coordinates, then uses XGBoost for prediction.
AI.result: SAGE-XGBoost consistently outperformed conventional and spatially explicit ML models, achieving ~33 percentage point improvement over Spatial XGBoost. AUC values: ~0.97 for landslide susceptibility and ~0.95 for wildfire susceptibility. Feature analysis confirmed graph embeddings' contribution and improved spatial coherence.
AI.conclusion: SAGE-XGBoost provides an efficient and transferable alternative to deep representation learning for environmental hazard assessment and geospatial prediction under limited supervision, with improved performance and spatial coherence.

title: Specification-delta-driven data governance: an empirical study of the «spec-delta» as the unit of change in lakehouse data platforms
summary: Spec Driven Development SDD has consolidated the idea that the specification rather than the code should be the primary artefact governing AI assisted work. Tools such as GitHub Spec Kit, and proposals such as Constitutional SDD, have formalised this principle in the software domain, while the executable data-contracts literature has extended it to schema and quality enforcement at run time. Nevertheless, the treatment of the specification delta OpenSpec's core idea that every change should produce a reviewable increment of requirements as the unit of change in data platforms remains empirically unexplored, even though many data-platform changes are contractual (new datasets, service-level agreements, metric semantics, access policies) rather than purely code changes. This work formalises the spec-delta concept, proposes a taxonomy of data platform changes according to their suitability for incremental specification, and defines a controlled experiment comparing a spec-delta-driven workflow against a conventional code pull-request workflow without a delta. The response variables are discovery to deployment time, the density of defects reaching the Silver and Gold lakehouse layers, cross-tool metric divergence, and reviewer cognitive load measured with NASA TLX. The paper explicitly reserves a demonstration-and-laboratory section for instantiation on a real lakehouse environment. The contribution is not a tool but reproducible evidence and an applicability guide that helps to avoid the up front over specification antipattern.

AI.tldr: Spec-Driven Development (SDD) introduces spec-deltas as the primary unit of change in data platforms, with empirical evidence showing improvements over conventional workflows.
AI.motivation: Data platform changes are often contractual (datasets, SLAs, metrics, policies) rather than just code changes, but current approaches lack empirical exploration of treating specification deltas as the primary unit of change. Existing tools have formalized SDD in software, but its application to data platforms with measurable outcomes remains unstudied.
AI.method: Formalizes the spec-delta concept, creates taxonomy of data platform changes based on incremental specification suitability, conducts controlled experiment comparing spec-delta-driven workflow vs conventional code pull-request workflow, measures time from discovery to deployment, defect density in lakehouse layers, cross-tool metric divergence, and reviewer cognitive load using NASA TLX.
AI.result: The paper promises empirical results but the abstract doesn't include specific quantitative findings. It indicates there will be reproducible evidence comparing the two approaches across multiple dimensions including deployment time, defect rates, metric consistency, and cognitive load. A demonstration on real lakehouse environment is reserved.
AI.conclusion: The contribution is not a tool but reproducible evidence and an applicability guide to help avoid upfront over-specification antipatterns. The work aims to provide empirical validation for spec-delta approaches in data platforms and guidance for practical implementation.

title: A Locally Tokenized Generative Model for Robust Time-Series Watermarking
comment: Submitted to NeurIPS 2026
summary: Watermarking is a central tool for provenance in generative models, yet its application to multivariate time series remains hindered by reliability failures under post-editing attacks. We show that existing detectors, which rely on globally coupled re-encoding, suffer from bidirectional drift of the null distribution: post-editing attacks can shift the z-score of non-watermarked samples in either direction, invalidating clean-calibrated thresholds. We argue that this instability is a property of the re-encoding, and that reliable detection requires each recovered unit to depend only on a bounded temporal neighborhood. Guided by this principle, we propose L-VQVAE, a generative model in which each discrete token is produced from a short contiguous window, and LVQMark, a watermarking method over this token space that combines logit-bias injection with robust re-encoding for attack-time detection. Experiments on four benchmarks spanning finance, energy, and neuroimaging show that our approach preserves generation quality while stabilizing both detection power and false-positive behavior under post-editing attacks.

AI.tldr: Proposes L-VQVAE and LVQMark, a new watermarking approach for multivariate time series that maintains reliable detection under post-editing attacks by using bounded temporal neighborhoods instead of globally coupled re-encoding.
AI.motivation: Existing watermarking methods for multivariate time series fail under post-editing attacks due to globally coupled re-encoding, which causes bidirectional drift in null distribution that invalidates clean-calibrated detection thresholds.
AI.method: Developed L-VQVAE, a generative model producing discrete tokens from short contiguous windows, and LVQMark, a watermarking method that combines logit-bias injection with robust re-encoding for attack-time detection, ensuring each recovered unit depends only on bounded temporal neighborhoods.
AI.result: Experiments on four benchmarks (finance, energy, neuroimaging) show the approach preserves generation quality while stabilizing both detection power and false-positive behavior under post-editing attacks.
AI.conclusion: Reliable watermarking for multivariate time series requires moving away from globally coupled re-encoding to bounded temporal neighborhood approaches to maintain detection reliability under post-editing attacks.

title: SAPO: Single-Rollout Autoregressive Policy Optimization for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) has become a critical stage in the post-training of large language models. Existing critic-free, group-relative methods estimate policy advantages from multiple rollouts, avoiding the substantial memory overhead of conventional proximal policy optimization (PPO) and achieving strong performance on long-horizon interactive tasks. Despite their success, recent studies revealed three limitations: (1) Lack explicit value generalization and effective temporal credit assignment; (2) Suffer from potential advantage collapse in long-horizon complex tasks; (3) Require a costly trade-off between sampling budget and policy performance. In this work, we propose Single-rollout Autoregressive Policy Optimization (SAPO), a low-memory and compute-efficient framework in which the policy and value functions share a single autoregressive backbone. SAPO exploits the autoregressive structure of LLMs to produce policy and value predictions at distinct causal boundaries with shared parameters, while independently optimizing the PPO objectives and auxiliary on-policy SARSA objectives. To robustly estimate the contribution of each turn, we further introduce a trajectory-level generalized advantage estimator that combines lambda-returns with batch normalization. Experiments across ALFWorld and WebShop with Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B show that SAPO trains stably and outperforms PPO and GRPO by mean +15.1 and +12.1 percentage points, respectively, while eliminating the memory cost of a separate critic model and reducing per-iteration runtime by 33.2% over PPO.

AI.tldr: SAPO is a single-rollout autoregressive policy optimization framework for LLM post-training that shares policy and value functions in one backbone, reducing memory/Compute while outperforming PPO and GRPO on interactive tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing critic-free group-relative RL methods for LLM post-training have three key limitations: lack explicit value generalization and temporal credit assignment, suffer from advantage collapse in long-horizon tasks, and require trade-offs between sampling budget and performance.
AI.method: SAPO shares policy and value functions in a single autoregressive LLM backbone, producing predictions at distinct causal boundaries. It optimizes PPO objectives plus auxiliary on-policy SARSA objectives, with a trajectory-level generalized advantage estimator combining lambda-returns and batch normalization.
AI.result: SAPO outperforms PPO and GRPO by +15.1 and +12.1 percentage points respectively on ALFWorld and WebShop tasks using Qwen2.5 models, eliminates separate critic memory cost, and reduces per-iteration runtime by 33.2% over PPO.
AI.conclusion: SAPO provides an efficient, stable framework for agentic RL in LLM post-training that addresses limitations of existing methods while offering better performance and lower computational costs.

title: RecPFN: Prior-Fitted Networks for In-Context-Based Recommendations
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures, 8 tables
summary: We introduce RecPFN, a prior-fitted network that brings in-context learning to sequential recommendation. RecPFN is pretrained entirely on synthetic clickstream environments sampled from a broad structural causal prior, enabling it to amortize Bayesian-style inference from a small support set. At inference, a lightweight decoder-only transformer conditions on a handful of domain sequences and produces next-item predictions for queries in a single forward pass, without any weight updates. Across eight public benchmarks, RecPFN achives state-of-the-art zero-shot performance while remaining strongly competitive with supervised methods in low-compute and low-data regimes. It is deployment-efficient and robust to domain shift, outperforming strong zero-shot baselines that rely on large real-interaction corpora. RecPFN provides a practical path toward generalizable, data-efficient recommenders and opens avenues for richer priors, longer-context ICL, and multimodal extensions. Code for training and evaluation is publicly available at https://github.com/SAP-samples/tabular-ai-recpfn/.

AI.tldr: RecPFN is a prior-fitted network for sequential recommendation that uses in-context learning, pretrained on synthetic clickstream data, enabling zero-shot state-of-the-art performance without weight updates.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to address the need for data-efficient, generalizable recommender systems that can work well in low-data regimes and be robust to domain shifts, moving beyond methods that require large real-interaction corpora.
AI.method: RecPFN is pretrained entirely on synthetic clickstream environments sampled from a broad structural causal prior. It uses a lightweight decoder-only transformer that conditions on a handful of domain sequences at inference time, producing next-item predictions in a single forward pass without weight updates.
AI.result: Across eight public benchmarks, RecPFN achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot performance while remaining strongly competitive with supervised methods in low-compute and low-data regimes. It outperforms strong zero-shot baselines that rely on large real-interaction corpora.
AI.conclusion: RecPFN provides a practical path toward generalizable, data-efficient recommenders and opens avenues for richer priors, longer-context in-context learning, and multimodal extensions.

title: PolicyGuide: From Guarding One Action to Guiding the Whole Workflow for Policy-Compliant LLM Agents
comment: 26 pages, 15 figures, including appendices
summary: Customer-service LLM agents must follow organizational policy when acting on a user's behalf. Compliance failures arise from either forbidden actions, such as granting an ineligible change, or omitted procedural requirements, such as identification or confirmation. Runtime safeguards can intervene on risky actions, but action-local checks do not guide an agent through a multi-step procedure. Workflow-following systems support prescribed process execution, but primarily target workflow completion rather than safeguarding agent behavior. PolicyGuide instead compiles each domain policy into a workflow graph and invokes a proactive verifier at user-turn boundaries. From persisted graph state, the verifier reconciles open requests and returns step-specific remediation along a policy-compliant path. Across the $τ^2$-bench airline, retail, and telecom domains with a GPT-5.4 agent and verifier, PolicyGuide raises mean $\mathrm{Pass}^4$ from $0.42$ to $0.62$, with the largest gain on telecom ($0.19$ to $0.61$), the most workflow-structured domain. The same workflows transfer to Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Gemini 2.5 Pro agents. Complementary evaluations find the lowest observed attack-success rate under adversarial users and the strongest procedural compliance in an author-designed workflow-level validation.

AI.tldr: PolicyGuide is a system that compiles domain policies into workflow graphs to guide LLM agents through multi-step procedures, using proactive verification at conversation boundaries to ensure policy compliance.
AI.motivation: Customer-service LLM agents often fail to follow organizational policies, either by performing forbidden actions or omitting required procedural steps. Existing approaches have limitations: runtime safeguards only check individual actions locally, while workflow systems focus on completion rather than safeguarding agent behavior.
AI.method: PolicyGuide compiles each domain policy into a workflow graph. At user-turn boundaries, it invokes a proactive verifier that reconciles open requests from persisted graph state and returns step-specific remediation along policy-compliant paths.
AI.result: Across τ²-bench domains (airline, retail, telecom) with GPT-5.4, PolicyGuide raises mean Pass⁴ from 0.42 to 0.62, with telecom showing the largest gain (0.19 to 0.61). Workflows transfer to Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Gemini 2.5 Pro. PolicyGuide shows lowest attack-success rate under adversarial users and strongest procedural compliance in workflow-level validation.
AI.conclusion: PolicyGuide effectively bridges the gap between policy compliance and workflow execution for customer-service LLM agents by converting policies into enforceable workflow graphs with proactive verification, significantly improving compliance across multiple domains and models.

title: Truncate Bad, Upweight Good: BoN-Style Distillation via Rank-Based Classification
summary: Inference-time selection methods, such as Best-of-N, improve generation by sampling a pool of candidates and selecting the top-ranked completion according to a reward model. Distillation seeks to amortize this procedure into a single policy by replacing raw rewards with in-pool ranks and learning a policy that upweights higher-ranked completions. However, existing rank-based policies typically use smooth full-support reweighting, so low-ranked completions receive less mass but remain in the target support. Although a sharper reweighting reduces lower-tail mass, it also increases reliance on brittle ranking at the top made by a single reward model. We propose TUP: a Truncate-bad, Upweight-good Policy that removes low-ranked completions from the support and reweights only the retained upper tail with a tunable sharpness. TUP admits a closed-form, prompt-independent normalization and can be trained fully offline via binary cross-entropy, using shifted-truncated win-rates as soft labels and distilled-to-reference log-likelihood ratios as logits. Theoretically, under certain assumptions, we show that for any unknown oracle reward, the best monotone rank-reweighting can be matched by a lower-tail truncation rule, providing formal support for removing the lower tail rather than merely downweighting it. Empirically, we show that TUP is competitive with strong offline alignment baselines.

AI.tldr: TUP (Truncate-bad, Upweight-good Policy) is a new distillation method that removes low-ranked completions entirely rather than just downweighting them, using binary cross-entropy with soft labels based on win-rates for more robust offline policy learning.
AI.motivation: Existing rank-based distillation methods use smooth reweighting where low-ranked completions still receive some probability mass, which may not be optimal. While sharper reweighting could reduce lower-tail mass, it increases reliance on brittle top-ranking decisions from a single reward model.
AI.method: TUP truncates low-ranked completions from the support entirely and reweights only the retained upper tail with tunable sharpness. It uses binary cross-entropy training with shifted-truncated win-rates as soft labels and distilled-to-reference log-likelihood ratios as logits, admitting a closed-form, prompt-independent normalization.
AI.result: Empirically, TUP shows competitive performance with strong offline alignment baselines. Theoretically, it's shown that for any unknown oracle reward, the best monotone rank-reweighting can be matched by a lower-tail truncation rule, providing formal justification for removing rather than merely downweighting the lower tail.
AI.conclusion: TUP offers a more effective approach to policy distillation by completely removing low-quality completions rather than just downweighting them, combining theoretical justification with practical effectiveness through its truncate-and-reweight strategy.

title: EnvHarness: Awakening Static Worlds for Agent Learning
summary: LLM agents learn by interacting with environments, yet these environments are hand-built and static: blind to an agent's weaknesses, and quickly left behind as it improves. While recent environment generation methods attempt to address this, they require domain-specific pipelines, rely on expensive or unreliable verifiers, and still produce static environments. To alleviate the engineering burden of rebuilding environments from scratch, we propose Environment Harness (EnvHarness), a programmable layer of plug-in components that wraps a static environment to reshape its behavior without modifying the underlying logic. Operating through standard interfaces, EnvHarness applies across diverse domains while ensuring every reshaped environment retains its original verifier. To automate this process, we introduce EnvRigger, which treats the target policy as a black box, observing its execution trajectories to synthesize EnvHarness components targeting diagnosed flaws, and validating them via fresh rollouts. Across five benchmarks in four domains, EnvHarness outperforms both original environments and domain-specific environment generation pipelines, achieving up to a 9.0-point improvement on held-out instances with 9.8% fewer execution steps. Furthermore, EnvHarness provides a superior optimization signal for reinforcement learning, enabling continuous, targeted co-evolution of the policy and its environment.

AI.tldr: EnvHarness: A programmable plug-in system for dynamically reshaping static environments for LLM agents, with EnvRigger automating component synthesis to target policy weaknesses, outperforming domain-specific generation methods.
AI.motivation: Current environments for LLM agents are static and hand-built, making them blind to agent weaknesses and quickly outdated as agents improve. Existing environment generation methods require domain-specific pipelines, rely on expensive verifiers, and still produce static environments. There's a need to reduce the engineering burden of rebuilding environments from scratch.
AI.method: Propose Environment Harness (EnvHarness) - a programmable layer of plug-in components that wraps static environments to reshape behavior without modifying underlying logic. Introduce EnvRigger to automate component synthesis by treating target policy as black box, observing execution trajectories to diagnose flaws and validate via fresh rollouts. Uses standard interfaces for cross-domain applicability.
AI.result: Outperforms both original environments and domain-specific environment generation pipelines across five benchmarks in four domains. Achieves up to 9.0-point improvement on held-out instances with 9.8% fewer execution steps. Provides superior optimization signal for reinforcement learning, enabling continuous, targeted co-evolution of policy and environment.
AI.conclusion: EnvHarness offers a flexible, automated approach to environment generation that reduces engineering burden while enabling dynamic co-evolution of agents and their environments, outperforming static and domain-specific alternatives.

title: Credit Without Ground Truth: Auditing Step-Level Credit Assignment in LLM Agents Against Executed Replay
comment: 49 pages, 7 figures. Pre-registered; frozen analysis plans and prompts included in the appendices. Under review
summary: Audited against causal ground truth from executed replay in a single-agent tool environment (ALFWorld), none of the step-level credit signals used to train LLM agents -- LLM-judge scores, outcome-conditioned logprob ratios, or the policy's own confidence -- identifies which steps causally matter better than chance. Existing evaluations grade these signals against annotated step *correctness*; we audit them against step *contribution* -- what re-sampling the policy's own alternatives at each decision point and rolling forward actually changes about the outcome -- and the two come apart. The ground truth itself is structured: causal contribution is sparse (30.5% of decision points where ground truth is defined carry measurable effect), and measurability is model-dependent -- the fraction of points with no policy-supported counterfactual differs by a factor of two (13.1% vs. 26.8%) between two similar-scale policies. The failure mode is identifiable: implicit credit echoes the policy's fluency (median rank correlation +0.75, replicating at +0.70 in a second family under a corrected instrument), while conditioning on the outcome adds no causal information (partial correlation -0.004, Qwen). A confidence-only router recovers pivotal steps at chance level, but cuts judge cost by 13.1% per turn (14.0% per trajectory). In a seven-arm pre-registered training experiment, no arm reliably outperforms the untrained policy, and the checkpoints' apparent instrument signature is fully explained by training dose -- sparser credit retains fewer examples, an order-of-magnitude spread in optimizer steps -- not credit content. Comparisons of credit rules must therefore match effective sample size, or they measure dose, not credit.

AI.tldr: Existing step-level credit signals used to train LLM agents fail to identify which steps causally matter better than chance when audited against causal ground truth in tool-use environments.
AI.motivation: Current evaluations of LLM agent training signals focus on step correctness rather than step contribution to outcomes. The paper aims to audit whether existing credit signals (LLM-judge scores, outcome-conditioned logprob ratios, policy confidence) can actually identify which steps causally affect outcomes.
AI.method: Used causal ground truth from executed replay in ALFWorld single-agent tool environment. Audited credit signals against step contribution (what changes when re-sampling policy's alternatives at each decision point). Analyzed structure of ground truth, failure modes, and conducted 7-arm pre-registered training experiment controlling for effective sample size.
AI.result: None of the tested credit signals identifies causally important steps better than chance. Causal contribution is sparse (30.5% of decision points matter). Measurability differs between policies. Implicit credit echoes policy fluency (median rank correlation +0.75), outcome conditioning adds no causal information. Confidence-only routing cuts judge cost by 13.1% per turn but performs at chance level. Training experiments show no improvement over untrained policy when controlling for effective sample size.
AI.conclusion: Step correctness and step contribution are different evaluation metrics. Existing credit signals fail to identify causal contribution. Comparisons must control for effective sample size (training dose) to avoid measuring dosage rather than credit quality. There's a need for causally meaningful credit signals.

title: TESTNAV: Pareto-Guided Search for Compositional Robustness Testing
summary:
Deep learning models remain vulnerable to real-world input perturbations, especially when multiple corruptions co-occur in the same input (e.g., brightness shifts and motion blur). Compositional testing reveals these interaction effects but introduces two challenges: combinatorial growth of the perturbation space as dimensions and severity levels increase, and uneven diagnostic value-many combinations yield unrealistically degraded inputs with limited practical relevance.
  We present TESTNAV, 1 a Pareto-guided robustness testing framework for efficiently exploring discrete, compositional perturbation spaces when only a limited number of perturbation configurations can be evaluated. TESTNAV prioritises severe yet realistic failures by formulating robustness testing as bi-objective optimisation: maximise performance degradation while preserving input fidelity measured by modality-specific metrics (e.g., SSIM and KID for vision; chrF and BERT-F1 for language and code). It uses NSGA-II to approximate the bi-objective Pareto front. Across four benchmarks spanning vision, natural language, and code generation, TESTNAV recovers Pareto fronts up to 2.15x faster than search-based baselines, using 35.8%-89.3% of the discrete perturbation space defined by four perturbation dimensions with six levels each.

AI.tldr: TESTNAV is a Pareto-guided robustness testing framework that efficiently explores compositional perturbation spaces by balancing performance degradation against input fidelity, using NSGA-II to find severe yet realistic failures.
AI.motivation: Deep learning models are vulnerable to real-world input perturbations, especially when multiple corruptions co-occur. Compositional testing reveals interaction effects but faces challenges: combinatorial explosion of perturbation space and uneven diagnostic value where many combinations create unrealistically degraded inputs with limited practical relevance.
AI.method: TESTNAV formulates robustness testing as bi-objective optimization: maximize performance degradation while preserving input fidelity measured by modality-specific metrics (SSIM and KID for vision; chrF and BERT-F1 for language and code). It uses NSGA-II (Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II) to approximate the bi-objective Pareto front for efficiently exploring discrete, compositional perturbation spaces.
AI.result: Across four benchmarks spanning vision, natural language, and code generation, TESTNAV recovers Pareto fronts up to 2.15x faster than search-based baselines, using only 35.8%-89.3% of the discrete perturbation space defined by four perturbation dimensions with six levels each.
AI.conclusion: TESTNAV provides an efficient framework for robustness testing that prioritizes severe yet realistic failures by balancing performance degradation with input fidelity, effectively addressing the combinatorial explosion problem in compositional perturbation testing while maintaining practical relevance.

title: Finite-Horizon Input-Output Dynamics of Minibatch Perturbations in AdamW
summary: A minibatch can influence training beyond the update at which it is observed because AdamW stores past gradient information in its optimizer states. We study this delayed effect through paired trajectories that differ only in one gradient update and share the same subsequent training sequence. We formulate AdamW as a finite-horizon input--state--output (ISO) system whose state contains the model parameters and first- and second-moment estimates. Linearizing the joint dynamics yields a signed response operator that maps a localized gradient perturbation to its future loss effects, revealing how optimizer memory shapes their magnitude, timing, and sign. We further derive an exact multistep error decomposition and establish first-order finite-horizon accuracy under local smoothness and controlled activation switching. Experiments validate the response mechanism and optimizer-state effects, while repeated-future analyses reveal substantial prospective structure in delayed influence that can be partially recovered from ISO approximations. Code is available at https://github.com/Kanyooo/Loss_ISO.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how individual minibatches influence future training in AdamW through optimizer state memory, formulating AdamW as an ISO system to study delayed gradient effects on loss.
AI.motivation: Minibatches in AdamW can influence training beyond their immediate update because AdamW stores past gradient information in its optimizer states (first and second moments). There's a need to understand this delayed effect of gradient perturbations on future loss trajectories.
AI.method: The authors study paired training trajectories that differ only in one gradient update. They formulate AdamW as a finite-horizon Input-State-Output (ISO) system where state includes model parameters and moment estimates. They linearize the joint dynamics to create a signed response operator mapping gradient perturbations to future loss effects, derive an exact multistep error decomposition, and establish first-order finite-horizon accuracy under certain conditions.
AI.result: Experiments validate the response mechanism and optimizer-state effects. The analysis reveals substantial prospective structure in delayed influence that can be partially recovered from ISO approximations. The signed response operator shows how optimizer memory shapes the magnitude, timing, and sign of future loss effects.
AI.conclusion: AdamW's optimizer memory creates delayed effects of minibatches on training trajectories. The ISO framework provides mathematical tools to analyze these effects, revealing how localized gradient perturbations propagate through the optimization process, with implications for understanding optimization dynamics and potentially improving training strategies.

title: Write Once, Run Everywhere: The Axon DSL for Shape-Safe and Framework-Agnostic LLM Architectures
summary: The entire ecosystem of open-source language models effectively relies on a single platform. What if this platform was forced to shut down tomorrow? Implementing and maintaining efficient model definitions and translating them between different training and inference regimes is a resource-heavy task that severely limits model efficiency and portability, hindering both scaling and deployment. Here, we present Axon, a strongly typed domain-specific language with Haskell-like syntax, that enables a write-once, run everywhere paradigm for LLM architectures. By basing collaboration on a language specification rather than a specific framework's vision, Axon fosters open cooperation and empowers researchers to implement highly specialized architectures without giving up optimization infrastructure or accepting deployment lock-in. Axon allows for concise, auditable specifications that can be automatically compiled to standalone implementations for leading frameworks: PyTorch, PyTorch with Triton, JAX, MLX and vLLM. In 467 inference benchmarking experiments on models ranging from 135M to 32B parameters, we demonstrate median speedups of 7% on PyTorch, 12% on PyTorch with Triton, 91% on JAX, and 107% on MLX, compared to the reference implementations from Transformers. When deployed as native vLLM architectures with PagedAttention and KV-cache, Axon models achieve a 58% median speedup over Transformers implementations.

AI.tldr: Axon is a strongly-typed DSL for LLM architectures that enables write-once, run-everywhere portability across frameworks, achieving significant speedups over reference implementations.
AI.motivation: Current open-source LLM ecosystem relies on a single platform, creating dependency risk and resource-heavy maintenance. Model efficiency and portability are limited by framework-specific implementations, hindering scaling and deployment.
AI.method: Axon is a strongly typed domain-specific language with Haskell-like syntax that allows concise, auditable model specifications. These specifications can be automatically compiled to standalone implementations for multiple frameworks including PyTorch, PyTorch with Triton, JAX, MLX, and vLLM.
AI.result: In 467 inference benchmarking experiments on models from 135M to 32B parameters: median speedups of 7% on PyTorch, 12% on PyTorch with Triton, 91% on JAX, and 107% on MLX compared to Transformers. When deployed as native vLLM architectures with PagedAttention and KV-cache, Axon models achieve 58% median speedup over Transformers implementations.
AI.conclusion: Axon enables a write-once, run-everywhere paradigm for LLM architectures, fostering open cooperation and empowering researchers to implement specialized architectures without sacrificing optimization or accepting deployment lock-in.

title: Unsupervised Anomaly Detection Using Flow Matching on Tabular Data
summary: Financial anomaly detection often relies on large unlabeled transaction logs, where anomalous samples may already be present during training. Such training-set contamination violates the clean-normal data assumption underlying many anomaly detection methods. Although flow matching has demonstrated strong performance in generative modeling, its robustness in unsupervised tabular anomaly detection remains underexplored. In this work, we study flow-matching-based anomaly detection under contaminated training data by comparing Time-Conditioned Contraction Matching (TCCM) with Forest-Flow and evaluating multiple anomaly scoring functions. Our results show that the choice of anomaly score is critical. The original single-step Decision score used by TCCM is sensitive to contamination, whereas trajectory-based Deviation and Reconstruction scores provide more stable anomaly signals. With these scores, Forest-Flow becomes competitive with, and in some cases outperforms, TCCM. These findings highlight the importance of anomaly scoring for flow-matching methods in financial anomaly detection under severe class imbalance.

AI.tldr: Flow-matching methods for financial anomaly detection are evaluated under contaminated training data, showing that anomaly scoring functions significantly impact performance, with trajectory-based scores being more robust than single-step scores.
AI.motivation: Financial anomaly detection often faces training-set contamination where anomalous samples are present during training, violating the clean-normal assumption. Flow matching's robustness in unsupervised tabular anomaly detection with contaminated data remains underexplored.
AI.method: The study compares Time-Conditioned Contraction Matching (TCCM) with Forest-Flow under contaminated training data, evaluating multiple anomaly scoring functions including the original single-step Decision score, and trajectory-based Deviation and Reconstruction scores.
AI.result: The choice of anomaly score is critical - TCCM's original single-step Decision score is sensitive to contamination, while trajectory-based Deviation and Reconstruction scores provide more stable anomaly signals. With these better scores, Forest-Flow becomes competitive with and sometimes outperforms TCCM.
AI.conclusion: Anomaly scoring function selection is crucial for flow-matching methods in financial anomaly detection, especially under severe class imbalance and training data contamination, with trajectory-based scores offering greater robustness.

title: EXIMO: VLM Guided Exploration of VLA Policies
summary: How to efficiently finetune robot policies to learn new tasks on the fly? State of the art robotic manipulation policies are based on behaviour cloning of large vision-language-action (VLA) models with billions of parameters on huge teleoperation datasets. While this simple approach has enabled significant advances for robotic manipulation, finetuning of VLA policies for learning new tasks still remains an open problem. In particular, collecting teleoperation datasets requires hundreds of hours of expensive human labour and the alternative, reinforcement learning (RL), can be notoriously sample-inefficient especially for long-horizon tasks. In addition, RL with VLAs imposes several challenges due to the model's size and architectural design. In this work, we propose EXIMO, an efficient algorithm for finetuning of VLA policies. EXIMO operates in three stages: explore, imitate, and optimize. During the explore phase, EXIMO equips the VLA with a vision language model (VLM) that acts as a planner. The VLM thinks and breaks down challenging long-horizon problems into shorter ones for the VLA. The VLM, together with the VLA, is used to collect an orchestrated dataset on new tasks. During the imitate phase, the VLA is finetuned with the orchestrated data. Finally, during the optimize stage, we use residual off-policy RL to further finetune the policy. In our experiments, we ablate all three stages of EXIMO and show that it outperforms existing approaches significantly in terms of sample-efficiency and final performance.

AI.tldr: EXIMO is a three-stage algorithm (explore, imitate, optimize) that efficiently finetunes large vision-language-action models for robot manipulation by combining VLM planning, behavior cloning, and residual RL.
AI.motivation: Current VLA-based robotic policies require expensive teleoperation datasets for new tasks, while reinforcement learning is sample-inefficient for long-horizon tasks. Finetuning billion-parameter VLAs remains challenging due to their size and architecture.
AI.method: Three-stage approach: 1) Explore: Use VLM as planner to break long-horizon tasks into subtasks and collect orchestrated data. 2) Imitate: Finetune VLA with collected data. 3) Optimize: Apply residual off-policy RL for further improvement.
AI.result: EXIMO outperforms existing approaches in sample-efficiency and final performance, with ablation studies confirming the effectiveness of all three stages.
AI.conclusion: EXIMO provides an efficient solution for finetuning VLA policies on new robotic manipulation tasks without requiring expensive teleoperation data, addressing key challenges in sample efficiency for long-horizon problems.

title: MileGPO: Milestone Inference with Local Evidence for Graph-Based Policy Optimization of Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Credit assignment is challenging in long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning, where supervision often comes only from final rewards. Existing methods refine trajectory-level signals into step-level credits through step grouping or graph-based advantage estimation, but can overlook meaningful intermediate milestones. We propose MileGPO (Milestone Inference with Local Evidence for Graph-Based Policy Optimization), which derives process-level credit from grouped on-policy rollouts through three designs. Milestone Discovery identifies candidate milestones on successful rollouts and recurring traps on failed ones. Reliability-Calibrated Shaping (RCS) weights these candidates by outcome-based confidence, strengthening reliable milestones and traps while down-weighting uncertain ones. Progress-Contrastive Calibration (PCC) further tests whether a candidate reflects local progress and whether its incoming ansition outperforms observed alternatives from the same state.MileGPO requires neither auxiliary models nor additional environment interaction. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop show state-of-the-art performance and a small in-distribution to out-of-distribution gap on ALFWorld. Ablations and credit diagnostics indicate that reliability weighting, local progress, and same-state branch evidence complement milestone discovery and resolve ambiguous intermediate credit.

AI.tldr: MileGPO uses milestone discovery and reliability calibration to improve credit assignment in long-horizon reinforcement learning without needing additional models or environment interaction.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for credit assignment in long-horizon RL often overlook meaningful intermediate milestones, only providing trajectory-level or step-level credits without identifying important process-level structures.
AI.method: Three main components: 1) Milestone Discovery identifies candidate milestones on successful rollouts and recurring traps on failed ones; 2) Reliability-Calibrated Shaping weights these candidates by outcome-based confidence; 3) Progress-Contrastive Calibration tests whether candidates reflect local progress and whether their transitions outperform alternatives from same states.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks, with small in-distribution to out-of-distribution gap on ALFWorld. Ablations show that reliability weighting, local progress, and same-state branch evidence effectively resolve ambiguous intermediate credit.
AI.conclusion: MileGPO provides an effective framework for deriving process-level credit assignment without auxiliary models or additional environment interaction, addressing key limitations of existing methods for long-horizon agentic RL.

title: Bringing analytic rigor to agentic AI for science: The Brain Researcher platform for neuroimaging data analysis
comment: 103 pages, 19 figures; Supplementary Information included
summary: AI agents can execute scientific analyses, but an analytic output becomes a defensible claim only after alternatives are weighed and the claim is limited to what the evidence supports. Agents may reproduce failures including selective analysis, premature declarations of success and optimization of imperfect criteria. We present Brain Researcher, an agentic research harness operating in a neuroimaging researcher's computational environment under rules for admissible analyses, required checks and claim scope. In benchmarks, Brain Researcher increased first-choice tool-selection accuracy across seven models by 70.2 percentage points (23.3% without it versus 93.6% with it) and verifiable grounding from 4.6% to 22.0%. In collaborator-led and self-evolving studies, multiverse analyses exposed analytic-choice sensitivity, and scientific review classified claims as accepted, qualified, revised, blocked, rejected or deferred. By linking decisions to evidence and provenance, Brain Researcher embeds methodological judgment within the workflow, not after it.

AI.tldr: Brain Researcher is an agentic research harness for neuroimaging that embeds methodological judgment within workflows by enforcing rules for admissible analyses, required checks, and claim scope, significantly improving tool-selection accuracy and verifiable grounding.
AI.motivation: AI agents can execute scientific analyses but often reproduce human failures like selective analysis, premature declarations of success, and optimization of imperfect criteria. There's a need to ensure analytic outputs become defensible claims only after alternatives are weighed and claims are properly limited to what evidence supports.
AI.method: Developed Brain Researcher, an agentic research harness that operates in a neuroimaging researcher's computational environment under predefined rules for: 1) admissible analyses, 2) required checks, and 3) claim scope. The system links decisions to evidence and provenance, embedding methodological judgment within the workflow rather than after it.
AI.result: In benchmarks, Brain Researcher increased first-choice tool-selection accuracy across seven models by 70.2 percentage points (from 23.3% to 93.6%) and improved verifiable grounding from 4.6% to 22.0%. In collaborator-led and self-evolving studies, multiverse analyses exposed analytic-choice sensitivity, and scientific review classified claims as accepted, qualified, revised, blocked, rejected or deferred.
AI.conclusion: Brain Researcher successfully embeds methodological judgment within scientific workflows, transforming AI agents from mere analysis executors into systems that produce defensible scientific claims by systematically weighing alternatives, enforcing checks, and properly limiting claims to what evidence supports.

title: Answer-Level Trust Selection for Physical Vision-Language Reasoning
comment: Preprint
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) can estimate physical quantities such as duration, speed, and acceleration from visual observations, but existing benchmarks primarily assess overall model performance against annotated ground truth. In deployment, a key question is whether an individual prediction can be trusted when its ground truth is unavailable. Self-consistency alone may fail to capture important failure modes: a VLM may produce stable-but-wrong estimates or rely on textual priors rather than visual evidence. We formulate answer-level selective prediction for quantitative physical reasoning and propose Answer-Level Trust Selection (ATS), a post-hoc, model-agnostic framework for accepting or rejecting individual VLM predictions. ATS requires no fine-tuning, auxiliary verifier, or access to the model's internal logits. Instead, it aggregates eight interpretable behavioral diagnostic scores derived from repeated queries and controlled interventions into a unified trust score. We evaluate ATS in depth on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and across 20 VLM backbones, examining selective performance, diagnostic behavior, and targeted failure modes. Our results show that intervention-based diagnostics help identify stable-but-wrong and prior-tracking predictions that repeated agreement alone may miss. However, improved failure-case rejection can come at the cost of lower retention of correct predictions. ATS therefore complements model-level capability evaluation with answer-level reliability assessment for quantitative VLM predictions. Code will be released upon publication.

AI.tldr: ATS is a post-hoc framework for evaluating trustworthiness of individual VLM predictions on physical reasoning tasks without ground truth, using interpretable behavioral diagnostics from repeated queries and controlled interventions.
AI.motivation: Current VLM benchmarks only assess overall performance against ground truth, but in real deployment we need to know whether individual predictions can be trusted when ground truth is unavailable. Self-consistency alone may miss important failure modes like stable-but-wrong estimates or reliance on textual priors rather than visual evidence.
AI.method: ATS (Answer-Level Trust Selection) is a post-hoc, model-agnostic framework that aggregates eight interpretable behavioral diagnostic scores derived from repeated queries and controlled interventions into a unified trust score. It requires no fine-tuning, auxiliary verifier, or access to model's internal logits.
AI.result: ATS shows intervention-based diagnostics help identify stable-but-wrong and prior-tracking predictions that repeated agreement alone may miss. However, improved failure-case rejection comes at the cost of lower retention of correct predictions.
AI.conclusion: ATS complements model-level capability evaluation with answer-level reliability assessment for quantitative VLM predictions, providing a practical framework for trust evaluation in deployment scenarios without ground truth.

title: Spike-based Belief Propagation in Nonlinear Dynamical Systems
comment: Accepted at NCTA 2026 (18th Int'l Conf. on Neural Computation Theory and Applications), part of IJCCI 2026, Angers, France. Pre-peer-review submitted version
summary: This paper presents a Bayesian control framework that integrates spike-based dynamics with probabilistic inference for adaptive control. Bayesian inference is widely regarded as a core computational principle of brain function, providing a normative framework for perception, decision-making, and learning under uncertainty. By combining a biologically inspired spiking neural model with Bayesian inference principles, we propose a brain-like control algorithm capable of operating in uncertain environments. We use the mountain car parking problem as a benchmark with non-linear dynamics. Our results demonstrate that the proposed controller can successfully update states in real time and generate goal-directed action plans through spike-driven dynamics. The results highlight the proposed model's potential as a bridge between computational neuroscience and probabilistic control theory.

AI.tldr: A Bayesian control framework combining spiking neural dynamics with probabilistic inference enables brain-like adaptive control in uncertain environments, demonstrated on the mountain car parking problem.
AI.motivation: Bayesian inference is recognized as a core computational principle in brain function for perception, decision-making, and learning under uncertainty. The authors aim to bridge computational neuroscience and probabilistic control theory by developing a brain-like control algorithm that operates effectively in uncertain environments.
AI.method: The framework integrates biologically inspired spiking neural models with Bayesian inference principles. It combines spike-based dynamics with probabilistic inference for adaptive control, using the non-linear mountain car parking problem as a benchmark to evaluate performance.
AI.result: The proposed controller successfully updates states in real time and generates goal-directed action plans through spike-driven dynamics. The model effectively operates in uncertain environments while maintaining the biological plausibility of spiking neural networks.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates a promising bridge between computational neuroscience and probabilistic control theory, showing how spike-based Bayesian control can enable adaptive, brain-like algorithms for operating in uncertain environments with non-linear dynamics.

title: FAR-DPO: Feasibility-Aware and Robust Direct Preference Optimization for Cyclic Peptide Design
comment: 16 pages, 6 figures, and 7 tables. Includes supplementary materials
summary: Cyclic peptides are emerging as promising molecular scaffolds in drug discovery due to their high binding affinity and structural stability. However, extending generative models from linear to cyclic peptide design remains challenging, as cyclization sharply restricts the feasible design space through coupled geometric and biophysical constraints. Moreover, limited training data has led existing approaches to rely largely on zero-shot generation or post hoc filtering, resulting in low yields of feasible designs and limited control over multi-objective trade-offs. To address these limitations, we propose FAR-DPO (Feasibility-Aware and Robust Direct Preference Optimization), an architecture-agnostic framework that steers generative models toward structurally and biophysically feasible cyclic peptide designs, particularly for challenging targets. FAR-DPO integrates feasibility-aware preference construction with difficulty-aware group-robust optimization. Specifically, it constructs within-target preference pairs through feasibility-gated multi-objective dominance and adaptively reweights predefined difficulty groups according to their current preference losses. On the CPSea LNR benchmark, under a fixed generation budget, FAR-DPO increases overall success rate from 46.89% to 57.79% on PepGLAD and from 47.96% to 49.57% on PepFlow. These gains also extend to the hardest target quartile and are accompanied by more favorable best-per-target binding scores. Together, these results demonstrate FAR-DPO's effectiveness in improving feasibility and target-wise robustness.

AI.tldr: FAR-DPO is a novel framework that improves generative models for cyclic peptide design by incorporating feasibility-aware preferences and difficulty-aware robust optimization, significantly boosting success rates on challenging targets.
AI.motivation: Cyclic peptides are promising for drug discovery due to high binding affinity and stability, but existing generative models struggle with cyclic peptide design due to geometric and biophysical constraints from cyclization, limited training data, and poor feasibility control in current approaches.
AI.method: FAR-DPO (Feasibility-Aware and Robust Direct Preference Optimization) uses two key innovations: 1) feasibility-aware preference construction through multi-objective dominance with feasibility gating, and 2) difficulty-aware group-robust optimization that adaptively reweights predefined difficulty groups based on their preference losses.
AI.result: On the CPSea LNR benchmark with fixed generation budget, FAR-DPO increased success rates from 46.89% to 57.79% on PepGLAD and from 47.96% to 49.57% on PepFlow. Improvements extended to hardest target quartile with better per-target binding scores.
AI.conclusion: FAR-DPO effectively improves both feasibility and target-wise robustness for cyclic peptide design, demonstrating architecture-agnostic effectiveness in steering generative models toward structurally and biophysically feasible designs for challenging targets.

title: A Strong Linear Baseline for Whole-Heart Cardiac Shape Completion on CT, with an Open Eleven-Structure Statistical Shape Model
summary: Public cardiac cohorts annotate different subsets of the heart, so shapes from separate sources cannot be pooled without shared correspondence. Among released cardiac shape resources, none we identified carries the atrial appendage, pulmonary veins, and caval stumps as separate blocks in one mesh. Completion benchmarks also compare deep models against a least-squares projection onto shape modes, not the conditional estimator the same fitted model implies. We release an eleven- structure cardiac computed-tomography (CT) statistical shape model, built from 383 automatically labelled cases in 11 571-vertex correspondence, and compare completion estimators under one frozen internal split and endpoint. On a 76-case internal list held out from fitting, a closed-form conditional-Gaussian estimator reconstructed the missing non-chamber structures at 3.717 mm mean per-vertex error, averaged equally over one, three, five, and nine observed structures. A five-refit mask-conditioned graph variational autoencoder reached 5.248 mm and nearest-neighbour retrieval 8.931 mm. The paired difference was 1.531 mm (95% confidence interval 1.384 to 1.711), and the ordering held in a raw-coordinate sensitivity arm. Expert manual labels exist for 58 external CT cases, but our registered reference is close enough to score only five structures. There the closed-form estimator again had lower average surface distance, 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance, and Chamfer error for both completed atria. On a second public benchmark of 20 cases the reference was close enough for three of four completed structures, and the same ordering held there. Four structures have no expert reference. The released model and its completion operator support cohort-unification research on aligned CT, not clinical use.

AI.tldr: Released an 11-structure cardiac CT statistical shape model with 383 cases, showing that a closed-form conditional-Gaussian estimator outperforms deep learning models and nearest-neighbor retrieval for completing missing cardiac structures.
AI.motivation: Public cardiac cohorts have inconsistent annotations, lacking shared correspondence between structures like atrial appendage, pulmonary veins, and caval stumps. Existing completion benchmarks use inadequate baselines (least-squares projection) rather than proper conditional estimators from fitted models.
AI.method: Built an 11-structure cardiac CT statistical shape model from 383 automatically labeled cases with 11,571-vertex correspondence. Compared completion estimators including: 1) closed-form conditional-Gaussian estimator, 2) five-refit mask-conditioned graph variational autoencoder, and 3) nearest-neighbour retrieval, evaluated on 76 internally held-out cases.
AI.result: Closed-form conditional-Gaussian estimator achieved 3.717 mm mean per-vertex error, outperforming the graph VAE (5.248 mm) and nearest-neighbour retrieval (8.931 mm). The paired difference was 1.531 mm (95% CI: 1.384-1.711). This ordering held across internal tests, 58 external CT cases, and a second public benchmark of 20 cases.
AI.conclusion: The released statistical shape model and its closed-form conditional completion operator enable cardiac cohort unification research on aligned CT data. The conditional-Gaussian estimator provides superior reconstruction accuracy for missing non-chamber structures compared to deep learning approaches.

title: Adaptive Probabilistic Shielding by Learning MDPs for Safe Reinforcement Learning
comment: 19 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. To be published in the proceedings of RV 2026
summary: Probabilistic shielding is a technique for safe reinforcement learning (RL). Typically, a static observer -- called the shield -- constrains the learning agent's actions to those for which acting safely remains feasible. Traditionally, the shield is computed from the transition probabilities of the underlying Markov decision process (MDP). Thus, this technique is not applicable when the MDP model is not given a priori, which, unfortunately, is the case in typical RL applications. In this paper, we study the problem of computing a shield in the setting where the transition graph of the MDP is known, but the transition probabilities are unknown. Our approach integrates probabilistic shielding with online model learning: as the RL agent explores the environment, we estimate the transition probabilities. From this estimate, we compute a shield. While the shield may be conservative initially, it adapts as the model estimate becomes more precise. Thus, the shield improves in tandem with the RL agent. This paradigm of adaptive probabilistic shielding raises a number of challenges, such as when to recompute the shield and how to balance between exploration and safety during learning. We empirically evaluate multiple variants of this paradigm across several environments.

AI.tldr: Adaptive probabilistic shielding integrates online model learning with safety constraints for RL agents operating in environments with unknown transition probabilities.
AI.motivation: Traditional probabilistic shielding requires known transition probabilities, but in typical RL applications, the MDP model is not given a priori. This creates a gap between theory (where shielding can ensure safety) and practice (where unknown transition probabilities prevent shield computation).
AI.method: The approach integrates probabilistic shielding with online model learning: as the RL agent explores, the system estimates transition probabilities, computes shields from these estimates, and adapts the shield as the model becomes more precise. The shield recomputation strategy and exploration-safety balance are key design challenges.
AI.result: The authors empirically evaluate multiple variants of this adaptive probabilistic shielding paradigm across several environments, showing that shields can be computed and refined without prior knowledge of transition probabilities.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive probabilistic shielding enables safe RL in environments with unknown transition probabilities by integrating online model learning with safety constraints, allowing shields to improve alongside agent learning while addressing challenges like recomputation timing and exploration-safety tradeoffs.

title: Learning Early-to-Final Solution Consistency for MILP Acceleration
summary: Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) is a fundamental problem class in operations research and combinatorial optimization, with broad applications to industrial decision-making. Owing to their NP-hardness, however, modern solvers may struggle to find high-quality solutions for challenging MILP instances within practical time limits. Recent learning-based approaches seek to accelerate MILP solving by directly predicting high-quality solutions from static instance-level features, such as variable-constraint bipartite graphs. Yet accurate solution prediction from instance features alone is difficult, and these methods largely overlook the information revealed during the solver's search process. In this paper, we find that solutions produced at the early search stage of MILP solvers, which are computationally cheap to obtain, are often structurally close to the solutions found after full-budget search. Motivated by this observation, we propose a new solver-informed paradigm that shifts the learning target from variable assignment to early-to-final consistency: for each variable, we predict whether its early-stage assignment should persist in full-budget solutions. The predicted consistency naturally guides downstream search, for instance by fixing the assignments deemed consistent. At inference time, we further ensemble consistency predictions across multiple early-stage solutions to improve robustness. Experiments across four MILP benchmarks show our method improves prediction-guided search across diverse downstream pipelines. With Gurobi, our proposed method reduces the primal gap by 56.9% on average and closes it completely on combinatorial auction instances. Besides, we transferred the Gurobi-trained model zero-shot to SCIP without adaptation, achieving a 36.4% average gap reduction across benchmarks.

AI.tldr: A solver-informed MILP learning method that predicts variable consistency between early-stage and final solutions to guide search, achieving significant primal gap reductions across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Traditional MILP solving struggles with NP-hard instances, while existing learning methods overlook valuable information from the solver's search process and have difficulty predicting solutions from static features alone.
AI.method: Proposes learning early-to-final consistency predictions for variables using early-stage solver solutions, which are cheap to obtain. At inference, ensembles predictions across multiple early solutions to guide search via variable fixing.
AI.result: Reduces primal gap by 56.9% on average with Gurobi, completely closes gap on combinatorial auction instances. Zero-shot transfer to SCIP achieves 36.4% average gap reduction across benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Solver-informed learning that leverages early-stage search information for consistency prediction effectively accelerates MILP solving and transfers well across different solvers.

title: Inadvertent Context Leakage in Language Models
summary:
For AI agents to be useful beyond simple chat, they must hold sensitive user context such as calendars, credentials, health records, and financial data. We study whether the mere presence of such secrets in a model's context window introduces hidden correlations into the model's benign outputs, allowing reconstruction even when the model correctly refuses direct extraction. We further study whether an adversary can actively engineer prompts that amplify this effect, using the model as a covert carrier to transmit secrets through seemingly innocuous text. In both cases, this limited leakage is exploited using a novel adaptive attack that assumes black-box access to the underlying model.
  In controlled experiments across eight proprietary models, we find that 2-digit in-context secrets are reconstructed with near-perfect accuracy and 4-digit secrets at 82\% exact match, all from outputs the model produces in response to ordinary, non-adversarial requests. We observe that more capable models leak more: stronger instruction-following amplifies sensitivity to in-context secrets, suggesting leakage is a byproduct of capability as opposed to a patchable bug. We show this leakage enables two practical attacks: (1) a trained classifier that infers semantic predicates about user memories (e.g., health conditions, financial events) from routine natural-language outputs, and (2) an RL-trained adversary that extracts full Social Security Numbers from a production-style agent.

AI.tldr: AI models leak in-context sensitive data through correlations in benign outputs, enabling secret reconstruction via adaptive attacks on black-box models.
AI.motivation: AI agents need access to sensitive user data (calendars, credentials, health records, financial data) to be useful, but this creates a security risk where mere presence of secrets in context window may introduce hidden correlations into model outputs, enabling secret reconstruction even when models correctly refuse direct extraction.
AI.method: 1) Study whether presence of secrets in context window introduces hidden correlations into model outputs; 2) Study whether adversaries can engineer prompts to amplify leakage; 3) Develop novel adaptive attack assuming black-box access; 4) Conduct controlled experiments across eight proprietary models; 5) Measure reconstruction accuracy for 2-digit and 4-digit secrets; 6) Analyze relationship between model capability and leakage; 7) Demonstrate two practical attacks: trained classifier for semantic predicates and RL-trained adversary for Social Security Number extraction.
AI.result: 1) 2-digit in-context secrets reconstructed with near-perfect accuracy; 2) 4-digit secrets reconstructed at 82% exact match from ordinary, non-adversarial outputs; 3) More capable models leak more (stronger instruction-following amplifies sensitivity); 4) Leakage enables practical attacks: trained classifier can infer semantic predicates about user memories, and RL-trained adversary can extract full Social Security Numbers from production-style agents.
AI.conclusion: In-context secret leakage is a significant security vulnerability in AI models, where sensitive data can be reconstructed from benign outputs through hidden correlations. This leakage is not a patchable bug but a byproduct of model capability, making it a fundamental trade-off between functionality and privacy. The demonstrated practical attacks highlight serious security implications for AI agents handling sensitive user data.

title: Rethinking Patch Based Multivariate Time Series Forecasting with Semantic Structured Partitioning
summary: Multivariate time series forecasting (MTSF) is a fundamental task in many real world applications. Existing patch based forecasting methods generally fall into three categories: fixed partitioning, multi-scale partitioning, and extendable partitioning. Fixed partitioning often breaks meaningful temporal boundaries, multi-scale partitioning may introduce redundant representations across scales, and extendable partitioning improves flexibility but still lacks an explicit mechanism for organizing semantic structure and modeling interactions among heterogeneous temporal patterns. To address these limitations, we propose SCPaT, a Transformer based framework built on semantic structured partitioning. SCPaT first decomposes input sequences into semantically consistent units through adaptive semantic unit generation, then constructs a dynamic semantic graph to model directed dependencies among these units and organize them into higher order semantic blocks.
