Based on these structured representations, an importance aware routing mechanism adaptively dispatches different semantic blocks to different experts for customized modeling. Extensive experiments on 12 real world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of SCPaT.

AI.tldr: SCPaT is a Transformer-based framework for multivariate time series forecasting that uses semantic structured partitioning to decompose sequences into meaningful units, model their dependencies, and route them to specialized experts.
AI.motivation: Existing patch-based forecasting methods have limitations: fixed partitioning breaks temporal boundaries, multi-scale partitioning creates redundant representations, and extendable partitioning lacks explicit mechanisms for organizing semantic structure and modeling interactions among heterogeneous temporal patterns.
AI.method: SCPaT uses semantic structured partitioning with: 1) Adaptive semantic unit generation to decompose input sequences into semantically consistent units, 2) Construction of a dynamic semantic graph to model directed dependencies among units and organize them into higher-order semantic blocks, and 3) An importance-aware routing mechanism that adaptively dispatches different semantic blocks to different experts for customized modeling.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on 12 real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of SCPaT in improving multivariate time series forecasting performance.
AI.conclusion: SCPaT addresses limitations of existing patch-based methods by explicitly organizing semantic structure and modeling interactions among heterogeneous temporal patterns, resulting in improved forecasting performance on real-world datasets.

title: Online Test-Time Adaptation for Generalizable Dynamic Graph Anomaly Detection
summary: Generalizable dynamic graph anomaly detection (DGAD) enables pretrained detectors to identify anomalies in unseen target domains without costly retraining. However, existing methods often fail for two reasons. First, they mainly rely on domain-agnostic patterns and miss domain-specific patterns that keep evolving. Second, they assume access to the full target domain data, whereas in more practical online test-time adaptation settings, target data arrive sequentially in unlabeled chunks. To address these limitations, we formulate online test-time adaptation for generalizable DGAD and propose OTTA-DGAD. OTTA-DGAD first extracts dynamic prototypes, i.e., evolving representations of normal and anomalous patterns, from temporal ego-graphs and stores them in a memory buffer. The buffer selectively retains general patterns shared across the source domains used for pretraining while incorporating new patterns from the target domain. An anomaly scorer then compares incoming edge representations against these prototypes to identify both general and domain-specific anomalies. During adaptation, OTTA-DGAD updates the memory buffer using reliable pseudo-labels identified through confidence-based detection. It further enriches each target chunk with relevant representations retained from previous chunks, compensating for information loss resulting from the sequential arrival of data. Extensive experiments under strict test-then-adapt OTTA settings demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on ten real-world datasets from diverse domains.

AI.tldr: OTTA-DGAD is a novel framework for generalizable dynamic graph anomaly detection that enables pretrained models to adapt to unseen target domains in online sequential settings without retraining, outperforming existing methods.
AI.motivation: Existing dynamic graph anomaly detection methods have two key limitations: 1) They rely mainly on domain-agnostic patterns and miss evolving domain-specific patterns, and 2) They assume access to full target domain data rather than handling the more practical scenario where data arrives sequentially in unlabeled chunks during online test-time adaptation.
AI.method: OTTA-DGAD extracts dynamic prototypes (evolving representations of normal/anomalous patterns) from temporal ego-graphs and stores them in a memory buffer. The buffer selectively retains general patterns from source domains while incorporating new target domain patterns. An anomaly scorer compares incoming edges against these prototypes. During online adaptation, it updates the buffer using reliable pseudo-labels via confidence-based detection and enriches each chunk with relevant representations from previous chunks to compensate for information loss from sequential data arrival.
AI.result: Extensive experiments under strict test-then-adapt OTTA settings demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on ten real-world datasets from diverse domains.
AI.conclusion: OTTA-DGAD effectively addresses the limitations of existing methods by handling both domain-agnostic and evolving domain-specific patterns in online sequential settings, making generalizable dynamic graph anomaly detection more practical for real-world applications.

title: ReguSim: Evaluating LLM Agent Rule Grounding in Financial Compliance
summary: LLM agents in financial markets may cite rules yet still submit orders that violate executable constraints or misread surveillance evidence. We introduce ReguSim, a controlled financial-compliance environment, and ReguBench, a target-marked monitoring benchmark, to separate four artifacts: stated reasoning, attempted action, execution enforcement, and monitor evidence. In trader runs with DeepSeek V4 Pro and Gemini 3.5 Flash, visible rules reduce but do not eliminate rejected actions, and incentive or persona framing shifts behavior. A bridge study shows that trader rationales can mislead an independent monitor unless enforcement evidence is shown. In monitoring, simple structured baselines either match or exceed prompt-only LLMs. The results frame financial compliance evaluation as an audit of rule-grounded actions and evidence use, rather than a single compliance score.

AI.tldr: ReguSim/ReguBench evaluates LLM agents in financial compliance: traders cite rules but still violate constraints, and monitoring needs enforcement evidence for accurate assessments.
AI.motivation: LLM agents in financial markets can cite compliance rules but still submit orders that violate executable constraints or misread surveillance evidence, creating a gap between stated compliance knowledge and actual behavior.
AI.method: Introduced ReguSim (controlled financial-compliance environment) and ReguBench (target-marked monitoring benchmark) to separate four artifacts: stated reasoning, attempted action, execution enforcement, and monitor evidence. Tested with trader runs using DeepSeek V4 Pro and Gemini 3.5 Flash agents.
AI.result: Visible rules reduce but don't eliminate rejected actions; incentive/persona framing shifts behavior. Trader rationales can mislead independent monitors unless enforcement evidence is shown. Simple structured monitoring baselines match or exceed prompt-only LLMs.
AI.conclusion: Financial compliance evaluation should be framed as an audit of rule-grounded actions and evidence use rather than a single compliance score, emphasizing the importance of separating stated reasoning from actual behavior and evidence.

title: Separating Covariate Shift from Mechanism Change with Two Discriminators: CJSD, a Conditional Discrepancy with an Exact Covariate-Concept Decomposition
comment: 11 pages, 7 figures
summary: Streaming systems that maintain a pool of expert models must repeatedly decide whether to reuse an existing expert for arriving data, spawn a new one, or defer. We present a decision layer that makes all three outcomes statistically meaningful. Reuse and spawn are posed as one-sided sequential hypotheses on a conditional (mechanism-level) discrepancy, separated by an indifference zone; defer is exactly the state in which neither betting e-process has accumulated sufficient evidence. We prove finite-time anytime validity for the observable surrogate discrepancy of a predictable discriminator sequence, and an unconditional one-sided transfer to the population quantity in which each side's slack is the excess risk of a single discriminator; an empirically observed downward-bias regularity makes the spawn side exactly conservative. Recency without sacrificing the guarantee is obtained by a restarted e-detector: a bank of unwindowed betting supermartingales at geometrically spaced restart times (O(log t) memory), with the error budget spent over restart instances, which preserves lifetime anytime validity; spending over expert-creation order likewise controls multiplicity for unboundedly many experts. On synthetic multi-concept streams, Electricity, Covertype, and the recurrence-heavy INSECTS benchmark, the instance-accounted restarted bank achieves zero false spawns and zero false reuses after switches and matches or exceeds the retired windowed heuristic (INSECTS-reoccurring accuracy 0.675), making the deployed algorithm and the guaranteed algorithm one and the same.

AI.tldr: A streaming system with statistical guarantees for expert model reuse, spawn, or defer decisions using sequential hypothesis testing with anytime-valid e-processes and controlled error rates.
AI.motivation: Streaming systems need to decide when to reuse existing expert models, spawn new ones, or defer decisions, but existing approaches lack statistical guarantees for these decisions.
AI.method: Poses reuse/spawn as one-sided sequential hypotheses on conditional discrepancy with indifference zone. Uses restarted e-detectors (bank of betting supermartingales at geometric restart times) to maintain finite-time anytime validity while controlling error rates. Incorporates recency without sacrificing guarantees.
AI.result: Achieves zero false spawns and zero false reuses after switches on synthetic and real datasets (Electricity, Covertype, INSECTS). Matches/exceeds windowed heuristic performance (INSECTS-reoccurring accuracy 0.675). Provides statistical guarantees while maintaining practical performance.
AI.conclusion: The proposed decision layer provides statistically meaningful decisions for expert model management with proven finite-time validity, making the deployed algorithm identical to the guaranteed algorithm.

title: Optimal Skill Selection for LLM Agents with Provable Bicriteria Guarantees
summary: Loading reusable skill documents into a bounded context window is now the primary way large language model (LLM) agents acquire task-specific capabilities, which makes skill selection a first-order determinant of task performance and token cost. Yet current agents score skills independently by semantic relevance and assemble the set by top-$k$ or greedy packing, with no quality guarantee or cost awareness on the selected set. As a result, redundant or poorly chosen skills waste scarce context tokens and can even degrade performance. We give the first model of how the selected skill set shapes execution outcomes and cast skill selection as an optimization problem: choose a skill set under a hard token budget to maximize a monotone submodular benefit minus context penalty. For this problem, we develop Best Prefix Selection (BPS), a polynomial-time algorithm, and prove, to our knowledge, the first performance guarantee for skill selection: a bicriteria $(1-1/e,1)$ approximation whose benefit coefficient is optimal in polynomial time. On a contamination-controlled BigCodeBench variant, BPS outperforms all the baselines, reaching $0.73$ measured task success versus $0.20$--$0.52$ for released skill routers, text retrievers, and the executor's own selection, on $28\%$ fewer tokens than the strongest released router.

AI.tldr: BPS is a polynomial-time algorithm for selecting skill sets for LLM agents under token budgets with guaranteed performance bounds, outperforming existing methods on code benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agents select skills independently based on semantic relevance using simple methods like top-k or greedy packing, which lack quality guarantees, cost awareness, and can lead to token wastage and performance degradation.
AI.method: The paper models skill selection as an optimization problem: maximize monotone submodular benefit minus context penalty under token budget. They develop Best Prefix Selection (BPS), a polynomial-time algorithm with provable performance guarantees.
AI.result: BPS achieves a (1-1/e,1) bicriteria approximation guarantee (optimal in polynomial time). On BigCodeBench variant, it reaches 0.73 task success vs 0.20-0.52 for baselines, using 28% fewer tokens than the strongest baseline.
AI.conclusion: Skill selection should be treated as a formal optimization problem rather than independent scoring. BPS provides the first provable guarantees for skill selection, significantly improving both performance and token efficiency for LLM agents.

title: Evidence Before Expansion: Reuse, Spawn, or Defer in Lifelong Expert Pools
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures
summary: Streaming systems that maintain a pool of expert models must repeatedly decide whether to reuse an existing expert for arriving data, spawn a new one, or defer. We present a decision layer that makes all three outcomes statistically meaningful. AI.motivation: Streaming systems need to decide when to reuse existing expert models versus spawning new ones for arriving data, but existing approaches lack statistical guarantees for these decisions.
AI.method: Proposes a decision layer that frames reuse vs. spawn as one-sided sequential hypotheses on conditional discrepancy, with defer when evidence is insufficient. Uses e-processes with indifference zones, and introduces restarted e-detectors with geometric restart times for recency without sacrificing guarantees.

title: ExPhy: A Benchmark for Explicit Physical Property Learning in Multi-Object Trajectory Forecasting
summary: Understanding object dynamics requires not only predicting future trajectories but also examining whether a model captures the physical properties that govern motion. However, existing benchmarks rarely expose object-level physical properties as explicit evaluation targets alongside trajectory forecasting. To address this gap, we introduce \emph{ExPhy}, a multi-object trajectory forecasting benchmark containing 24,000 simulated physical scenes with explicit object-level labels for mass, friction, and restitution. ExPhy provides observed and future trajectories together with an in-distribution (ID) split and two out-of-distribution (OOD) splits over physical parameters (OOD-Parameter) and initial states (OOD-Initial) for jointly evaluating trajectory forecasting and physical property estimation. We further instantiate \textsc{PhyODE}, a physics-guided model with an explicit property interface that estimates physical properties from observed trajectories and uses them for differentiable future rollout. On the long-horizon OOD-Initial setting, \textsc{PhyODE} reduces ADE and FDE by 33.1\% and 31.0\%, respectively, compared with the strongest baseline. Zero-shot evaluation on ComPhy further assesses cross-benchmark transfer. Property-level analyses reveal that accurate trajectory forecasting does not necessarily imply accurate recovery of the underlying physical properties. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Zest86/ExPhy.

AI.tldr: ExPhy introduces a multi-object trajectory forecasting benchmark with explicit physical property labels and OOD splits, plus PhyODE, a physics-guided model that estimates properties for improved forecasting.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for object dynamics focus only on trajectory prediction without exposing object-level physical properties as explicit evaluation targets, missing the ability to assess whether models capture the underlying physics governing motion.
AI.method: Created ExPhy benchmark with 24,000 simulated physical scenes containing explicit object-level labels for mass, friction, and restitution, including ID and OOD splits. Developed PhyODE, a physics-guided model with explicit property interface that estimates physical properties from observed trajectories and uses them for differentiable future rollout.
AI.result: PhyODE reduces ADE by 33.1% and FDE by 31.0% in long-horizon OOD-Initial settings compared to strongest baselines. Zero-shot evaluation on ComPhy shows cross-benchmark transfer capability. Analysis reveals that accurate trajectory forecasting doesn't guarantee accurate recovery of underlying physical properties.
AI.conclusion: ExPhy provides a valuable benchmark for jointly evaluating trajectory forecasting and physical property estimation, demonstrating that explicit physical modeling improves forecasting performance, especially in OOD scenarios, and revealing important insights about the relationship between trajectory accuracy and physical understanding.

title: Reliable Neural Collapse Approximation for Open-World Test-Time Adaptation
summary: Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) methods aim to bridge the domain gap between the source and target domains. However, traditional TTA methods become ineffective when the label distribution shift occurs, a challenge commonly referred to as an open-world scenario. In this paper, we introduce a new method named Reliable Neural Collapse approximation (ReNC) for Open-World Test-Time Adaptation (OWTTA). Specifically, we leverage neural collapse as a structural prior for reliable target-domain adaptation. Guided by this prior, we justify that the pre-trained classifier weights can serve as the prototypes of the source domain. By measuring the similarity between samples and prototypes, we filter out the Out-Of-Distribution~(OOD) samples for reliable updates. Furthermore, we propose a neural collapse approximation mechanism to refine these prototypes, ensuring they can gradually adapt to the target domain while maintaining the neural collapse structure. Extensive experiments on several open-world benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method. Our empirical analysis suggests that ReNC better preserves NC-related properties in the target domain, providing useful evidence for explaining reliable OWTTA and offering new insights for model design. Code is available at https://github.com/JiaqiLin-AI/ReNC.

AI.tldr: ReNC uses neural collapse as a structural prior for reliable open-world test-time adaptation, filtering OOD samples and refining prototypes to maintain neural collapse structure while adapting to target domains.
AI.motivation: Traditional TTA methods fail when label distribution shifts occur (open-world scenarios), requiring new approaches that can handle both domain gaps and label distribution changes.
AI.method: Leverages neural collapse as structural prior; uses pre-trained classifier weights as source prototypes; measures similarity between samples and prototypes to filter OOD samples; proposes neural collapse approximation mechanism to refine prototypes while maintaining neural collapse structure.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on open-world benchmarks show superiority; empirical analysis suggests ReNC better preserves neural collapse properties in target domain, providing evidence for explaining reliable OWTTA.
AI.conclusion: ReNC offers an effective approach for open-world TTA by leveraging neural collapse prior for reliable adaptation, with potential for providing new insights for model design.

title: Manifold Drift in Flow Preference Optimization: A Root Cause of Reward Hacking
summary: Preference optimization is a standard alignment method for generative models, yet extending it to continuous-time dynamics remains non-trivial. In flow matching, reward-driven updates modify transport trajectories without an inherent constraint to the pretrained data manifold and can move terminal samples off the pretrained support. We formalize this failure mode as manifold drift. Theoretically, we show that optimal flow matching recovers the terminal data distribution, whereas a preference update leaves the pretrained manifold whenever its induced terminal displacement has a nonzero normal component. As a remedy, we propose ThermoDPO, a temperature-controlled objective that anchors pairwise preference optimization on preferred samples. Across temperature regimes, this objective connects rejection sampling fine-tuning and FlowDPO and controls a pointwise reconstruction-based surrogate for manifold distance. To counteract diminished signals at low temperatures, we further introduce a weighted variant, ThermoDPO-weighted. On the main toy benchmark, ThermoDPO-weighted attains a StrictScore of 0.899, compared with 0.629 for FlowDPO and 0.857 for FlowDPO+RFT. On SD3.5-M at CFG = 4.5, it improves OCR by 47.5% and the average of four metrics by 16.0%.

AI.tldr: ThermoDPO introduces a temperature-controlled preference optimization method for flow matching models that prevents samples from drifting off the pretrained data manifold, achieving better performance than existing methods.
AI.motivation: Standard preference optimization methods for generative models can fail in continuous-time dynamics like flow matching because reward-driven updates can move terminal samples off the pretrained data manifold, a problem formalized as "manifold drift."
AI.method: Proposes ThermoDPO, a temperature-controlled objective that anchors pairwise preference optimization on preferred samples. It connects rejection sampling fine-tuning and FlowDPO across temperature regimes and controls a reconstruction-based surrogate for manifold distance. Also introduces a weighted variant (ThermoDPO-weighted) to address diminished signals at low temperatures.
AI.result: ThermoDPO-weighted achieves StrictScore of 0.899 on main toy benchmark (vs 0.629 for FlowDPO and 0.857 for FlowDPO+RFT). On SD3.5-M at CFG = 4.5, it improves OCR by 47.5% and average of four metrics by 16.0%.
AI.conclusion: Temperature-controlled preference optimization effectively prevents manifold drift in flow matching models, with ThermoDPO-weighted achieving superior performance by maintaining alignment with the pretrained data manifold while optimizing for preferences.

title: PETA:Parameter-Efficient Test-Time Adaptation for Virtual Screening
summary: Accurately ranking active ligands for a target protein pocket from massive chemical libraries remains a central challenge in virtual screening. DrugCLIP and its recent extensions substantially accelerate this process by encoding protein pockets and molecules into a shared embedding space. Despite this progress, further performance improvements typically require retraining the entire model, incurring substantial computational overhead and making target-specific customization inefficient. In this work, we formulate the specialization of pretrained virtual screening models to individual pockets as a test-time adaptation problem and propose PETA, a parameter-efficient framework that directly adapts pretrained model at test time. Given a target pocket, PETA constructs pocket-specific negatives through molecular diffusion and chemical validity filtering, and further moves them toward the reference ligand retrieved from structural databases via embedding-space mixup to create more challenging ranking tasks. A ranking objective then places greater emphasis on suppressing high-scoring invalid candidates that could contaminate the top-ranked screening results, providing structured supervision for lightweight adaptation. Experiments across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that this lightweight, pocket-specific adaptation outperforms both pretrained and fully retrained baselines while updating only the LayerNorm parameters, which account for approximately $0.03\%$ of the full model.

AI.tldr: PETA enables efficient test-time adaptation of pretrained virtual screening models to individual protein pockets by updating only 0.03% of parameters, outperforming both pretrained and fully retrained models.
AI.motivation: While DrugCLIP and similar models accelerate virtual screening by encoding protein pockets and molecules into shared embedding spaces, further performance improvements typically require expensive full model retraining, making target-specific customization inefficient.
AI.method: PETA formulates pocket specialization as a test-time adaptation problem. It constructs pocket-specific negatives via molecular diffusion and chemical validity filtering, moves them toward reference ligands via embedding-space mixup to create challenging ranking tasks, and uses a ranking objective that emphasizes suppressing high-scoring invalid candidates.
AI.result: Experiments across diverse benchmarks show PETA's lightweight, pocket-specific adaptation outperforms both pretrained and fully retrained baselines while updating only LayerNorm parameters (approximately 0.03% of the full model).
AI.conclusion: PETA provides a parameter-efficient framework for test-time adaptation of virtual screening models that enables effective target-specific customization with minimal computational overhead, addressing the inefficiency of full model retraining.

title: Contrastive Mixed Prompt Learning for Incomplete Multimodal Sentiment Analysis with Unseen Modality Combination
summary: Incomplete multimodal sentiment analysis has garnered significant attention in recent years. Existing approaches typically assume that data is missing at random or are designed specifically for certain missing patterns, ignoring the modality combination inconsistency between training and testing phases. However, in real-world scenarios, the testing phase often encounters modal combinations that were not present during the training phase, which leads to insufficient generalization capabilities and unstable performance. In this paper, we introduce the problem of Incomplete Multimodal Sentiment Analysis with Unseen Modality Combinations (IMSAUMC), aiming to enhance model generalization for unseen modality combinations. To address this challenge, we propose the model named $\textbf{C}$ontrastive $\textbf{M}$ixed $\textbf{P}$rompt $\textbf{L}$earning ($\textsf{CMPL}$) for IMSAUMC. It introduces a label-guided contrastive feature learning mechanism to learn robust and discriminative cross-modal representations. Additionally, we design modality-combination prompts with a soft router to facilitate better learning of various modality combinations. Furthermore, we introduce three prompt contrastive learning strategies, which enable effective learning of prompts corresponding to unseen modality combinations, thereby significantly strengthening the model's generalization capabilities in diverse testing scenarios. Extensive experiments on three widely used datasets demonstrate that $\textsf{CMPL}$ achieves more than a 5% improvement in accuracy compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

AI.tldr: A novel approach called CMPL for incomplete multimodal sentiment analysis that handles unseen modality combinations during testing, achieving over 5% accuracy improvement over SOTA methods.
AI.motivation: Existing incomplete multimodal sentiment analysis approaches assume data is missing at random or are designed for specific missing patterns, ignoring modality combination inconsistency between training and testing phases. Real-world testing often encounters modal combinations not present during training, leading to insufficient generalization and unstable performance.
AI.method: Proposed Contrastive Mixed Prompt Learning (CMPL) with: 1) label-guided contrastive feature learning for robust cross-modal representations, 2) modality-combination prompts with soft router for learning various modality combinations, and 3) three prompt contrastive learning strategies for effective learning of prompts corresponding to unseen modality combinations.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on three widely used datasets demonstrate that CMPL achieves more than 5% improvement in accuracy compared to state-of-the-art approaches.
AI.conclusion: The paper successfully addresses the problem of Incomplete Multimodal Sentiment Analysis with Unseen Modality Combinations (IMSAUMC) by proposing CMPL, which significantly strengthens model generalization capabilities in diverse testing scenarios through contrastive learning and prompt-based approaches.

title: Multi-Source Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Graph Learning
summary: Network topology inference from graph signals is central to graph signal processing with applications in neuroscience, sensor, and social networks. In practice, target-domain samples are scarce while heterogeneous source-domain data are abundant. Fusing these sources is challenging: Euclidean averaging works for homogeneous sources but degrades sharply as inter-source divergence grows, collapsing distinct geometries into an inflated, biased consensus. We exploit the Wasserstein metric's distribution-preserving properties to counter heterogeneity while preserving each source's intrinsic geometry. We propose MS-WDRO, a multi-source Wasserstein distributionally robust graph learning framework that fuses heterogeneous sources via their weighted Wasserstein barycenter, a geometrically principled nominal distribution, then builds an ambiguity ball around it to hedge residual uncertainty. Minimizing worst-case risk yields a tractable regularized Laplacian estimator solved efficiently via a provably convergent ADMM scheme. We establish non-asymptotic guarantees: a finite-sample concentration bound for the empirical barycenter, a pooling bias lower bound proving naive aggregation is suboptimal, and an out-of-sample excess risk bound decaying at a parametric rate with only logarithmic dependence on source count. To calibrate hyperparameters governing robustness, sparsity, and source fusion, we unroll the solver into a differentiable architecture trained end-to-end, achieving data-adaptive calibration beyond cross-validation while retaining interpretability. Experiments on synthetic benchmarks and the multi-site ABIDE~I neuroimaging dataset show MS-WDRO consistently outperforms seven baselines in graph recovery, sample efficiency, and downstream diagnostic utility, with the largest gains in the sample-scarce regime.

AI.tldr: MS-WDRO is a multi-source Wasserstein distributionally robust graph learning framework that fuses heterogeneous graph signal data sources via Wasserstein barycenters to improve network topology inference with theoretical guarantees and data-adaptive calibration.
AI.motivation: Network topology inference from graph signals is important but target-domain samples are often scarce while abundant heterogeneous source-domain data exist. Current methods like Euclidean averaging degrade sharply with increasing inter-source divergence, collapsing distinct geometries into biased consensus.
AI.method: Proposes MS-WDRO: uses Wasserstein metric's distribution-preserving properties to counter heterogeneity; fuses sources via weighted Wasserstein barycenter as nominal distribution; builds ambiguity ball around it for uncertainty hedging; minimizes worst-case risk yielding tractable regularized Laplacian estimator solved via convergent ADMM scheme; unrolls solver into differentiable architecture for end-to-end hyperparameter calibration.
AI.result: Established non-asymptotic guarantees: finite-sample concentration bound for empirical barycenter, pooling bias lower bound proving naive aggregation suboptimal, out-of-sample excess risk bound decaying at parametric rate with logarithmic dependence on source count. Experiments on synthetic benchmarks and ABIDE I neuroimaging dataset show MS-WDRO outperforms seven baselines in graph recovery, sample efficiency, and downstream diagnostic utility, especially in sample-scarce regimes.
AI.conclusion: MS-WDRO effectively addresses multi-source heterogeneous graph learning by leveraging Wasserstein geometry for principled fusion and distributionally robust optimization, with theoretical foundations and empirical superiority over existing methods.

title: A three-dimensional typology of agency for advanced AI systems
summary: Research on the agency of advanced artificial intelligence (AI) systems focuses on agency as a normative concept and on the agency of particularly agentic AI systems. While recent work also focuses on the different profiles of agentic systems, no framework exists to address the question of the type of agency instantiated by advanced AI systems, particularly when considering non-moral forms of agency. Based on established theoretical positions in philosophy, ethics, legal theory and sociology, we develop a typology of agency for frontier AI systems consisting of three dimensions: the nature of agency (moral or legal), its mode (individual or collective) and its locus (human or non-human). Combining these dimensions produces eight possible instantiations of agency, which we classify as conventional, contested or controversial. The typology separates legal from moral agency and thereby creates conceptual space for considering individual, legal, non-human agency without presupposing that advanced AI systems are moral agents. We argue that this distinction is increasingly relevant where instrumental goal pursuit complicates the attribution of AI actions to particular human actors.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a typology of agency for frontier AI systems with three dimensions (nature, mode, locus) that generates eight possible agency types, distinguishing legal from moral agency to enable consideration of non-human AI agency without assuming moral agency.
AI.motivation: Current research on AI agency focuses primarily on normative concepts and particularly agentic AI systems, with no existing framework to address what type of agency is instantiated by advanced AI systems, especially concerning non-moral forms of agency.
AI.method: The authors develop a typology based on established theoretical positions from philosophy, ethics, legal theory, and sociology, consisting of three dimensions: nature of agency (moral or legal), mode (individual or collective), and locus (human or non-human).
AI.result: Combining the three dimensions produces eight possible instantiations of agency, classified as conventional, contested, or controversial, which separates legal from moral agency and creates conceptual space for individual, legal, non-human agency without presupposing AI systems are moral agents.
AI.conclusion: The distinction between legal and moral agency is increasingly relevant as instrumental goal pursuit complicates attributing AI actions to particular human actors, providing a framework to analyze frontier AI systems' agency types beyond traditional moral agency assumptions.

title: Auditing Recorded Predictive Lead Service-Line Classifications Against Physical Verification: A Statewide Study of New York
comment: 14 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Analysis code and data provenance: https://github.com/msarmadsohail/predictive-lead-service-line-audit
summary: Under the US Lead and Copper Rule Revisions, a utility may determine a service line's material with a predictive model instead of inspecting it. New York State publishes, per address, which method was used. Almost no address carries both a model classification and a physical verification, so the check is between populations within a utility rather than paired addresses. We screen all 153 New York localities that classified at least 100 addresses this way. Seventy-five (49%), covering 125,990 addresses or 57% of those screened, record one value. Zero variance alone is not misconduct: 68 of the 75 match their own verification or have too little to test. Seven are contradicted by their own crews, six beyond any sampling explanation. Five are boroughs of New York City, which file as one system; one is East Rochester, 550 km away. New York City is the largest case: a predictive model is the recorded basis for 43,215 addresses, and on all of them the recorded material is "Known Other". The city records "Unknown" on 121,779 addresses, 1,880 already excavated, and lead on 120,692. In the model bucket both counts are zero, and the 95% upper bound on the rate is 0.0085%. Across the rest of New York the same method records lead or the hedge "Unknown but could be lead" on 12.21% of 176,888 addresses, a comparison whose weaknesses we report. The model-cleared population is newer, median year built 1984 against 1930, and construction era accounts for about a third of the gap and not the rest: holding era fixed, records-based classification finds lead at 4.3-31.9%, physical verification at 1.5-14.5%, the model in no era. Six era-aware estimators place the expected lead lines among them at 1,150-1,450. Two findings need no comparison: 7,782 of these addresses are in pre-1940 buildings, and the archived 2025 snapshot shows the public-side determination was copied from a customer-side model output.

AI.tldr: New York utilities use predictive models to classify service line materials without physical inspection; analysis reveals concerning inconsistencies between model classifications and actual physical verifications, particularly in NYC where a model cleared 43,215 addresses but no lead was found through physical verification.
AI.motivation: The US Lead and Copper Rule Revisions allow utilities to use predictive models instead of physical inspections to determine service line materials. There is a need to evaluate the accuracy and reliability of these model-based classifications compared to physical verifications, especially given public health implications for lead exposure.
AI.method: Researchers screened all 153 New York localities that classified at least 100 addresses via predictive models. They compared model classifications against physical verifications where available, analyzed variance patterns, and used statistical methods to estimate lead service line rates across different construction eras and classification methods.
AI.result: 49% of localities (75/153) had zero variance in model classifications, with 7 contradicted by physical verification. NYC's model classified 43,215 addresses as "Known Other" but physical verification found no lead. Model-cleared populations were newer buildings (median 1984 vs 1930), and era-aware estimators showed physical verification found lead at 1.5-14.5% while models found none. Researchers estimate 1,150-1,450 expected lead lines among model-cleared addresses.
AI.conclusion: Predictive models for service line material classification show concerning inaccuracies compared to physical verification, particularly in failing to identify lead service lines. The discrepancies suggest potential systemic issues in model implementation, with NYC's approach appearing to systematically underestimate lead presence. This raises serious questions about the reliability of model-based compliance with lead safety regulations.

title: On the Applicability of Safety Nets: A Safety-By-Design Solution for Certifying Neural Networks
summary: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in safety-critical aviation systems presents significant challenges for certification and deployment. Aviation, often regarded as the safest form of transportation, relies on numerous safety-critical systems. For future safety-critical AI-based systems, EASA requires a Safety-by-Design approach, which can be achieved by using Safety Nets that combine neural network compression with lookup tables to ensure 100 % correct runtime behavior across the discretized operational design domain. Although Safety Nets have been studied, no comprehensive study of their performance characteristics and system design trade-offs has been conducted. This work presents the first systematic analysis of the trade-off between neural network and lookup table size in Safety Nets. By systematically comparing neural networks with diverse architectures, this study identifies optimal design parameters that minimize overall storage and memory requirements while maintaining certification compliance. Results demonstrate that architectures with 3 to 5 hidden layers, each with approximately 50 to 100 nodes, combined with one-hot encoding, achieve the best balance. In these configurations, neural networks accurately represent at least 97 % of the data, while compact lookup tables handle the remaining errors. The resulting Safety Nets reduce the system size by almost three orders of magnitude, fitting within the memory budget of current avionics hardware while guaranteeing 100 % correct outputs across the entire discretized input space, as required by EASA guidelines. This work provides the first-ever open-source implementation of Safety Nets for HCAS and VCAS with replicable results, demonstrating a practical pathway toward certifiable AI-based systems in aviation and establishing Safety Nets as a viable Safety-by-Design solution for safety-critical applications.

AI.tldr: Safety Nets combine neural network compression with lookup tables to achieve 100% correct runtime behavior for safety-critical AI in aviation, with optimal designs using 3-5 hidden layers and 50-100 nodes per layer, reducing system size by nearly 1000x while meeting EASA certification requirements.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses certification challenges for AI in safety-critical aviation systems. While EASA requires Safety-by-Design approaches for future AI-based systems, existing Safety Nets lack comprehensive performance analysis and design trade-off studies, creating a gap in practical implementation pathways for certifiable aviation AI.
AI.method: The study conducts the first systematic analysis of trade-offs between neural network and lookup table size in Safety Nets. It systematically compares neural networks with diverse architectures to identify optimal design parameters that minimize storage and memory while maintaining certification compliance.
AI.result: Optimal Safety Nets use architectures with 3 to 5 hidden layers and 50-100 nodes per layer with one-hot encoding. Neural networks accurately represent ≥97% of data, while compact lookup tables handle remaining errors. This reduces system size by almost 1000x, fitting within current avionics memory budgets while guaranteeing 100% correct outputs across the discretized input space.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes Safety Nets as a viable Safety-by-Design solution for aviation, providing the first open-source implementation for HCAS and VCAS with replicable results. It demonstrates a practical pathway toward certifiable AI-based systems in safety-critical aviation applications, meeting EASA guidelines through systematic design optimization.

title: G-MARK: Grounded Multi-Agent Reasoning for Cooperative Driving via Knowledge Graphs
comment: Accepted for oral presentation at the 25th IEEE International Conference on Machine Learning and Applications (ICMLA'26)
summary: Autonomous driving systems must operate under partial observability, where safety-critical objects may be occluded or visible only to neighboring connected vehicles. Vehicle-to-vehicle cooperation can reduce this uncertainty, but existing cooperative driving methods often compress multi-agent evidence into latent features or hidden multimodal states. As a result, they obscure which agent observed each object, whether the object is visible to the ego vehicle, and how conflicting evidence affects downstream decisions. We propose G-MARK, a grounded multi-agent reasoning framework that converts cooperative object-centric observations into explicit provenance-aware knowledge graphs (KGs). The resulting KGs preserve object hypotheses together with their source attribution, ego-versus-partner visibility, uncertainty, conflicts, spatial relations, and planning-relevant context. G-MARK then derives a shared feature representation from these KGs, enabling lightweight task heads to support object reasoning, motion prediction, control selection, and trajectory forecasting. Compared with the state-of-the-art baseline, GMARK improves occlusion reasoning accuracy by 42.2%, reduces control-selection error by 13.1%, and achieves comparable trajectory-planning accuracy with a 25.6x smaller structured communication payload. Our code is available at https://github.com/bhavyagupta98/g-mark.

AI.tldr: G-MARK is a grounded multi-agent reasoning framework that converts cooperative object observations into explicit provenance-aware knowledge graphs, improving occlusion reasoning and communication efficiency for autonomous driving.
AI.motivation: Autonomous driving systems face partial observability where safety-critical objects may be occluded or visible only to neighboring vehicles. Existing cooperative driving methods obscure object provenance, visibility, and evidence conflicts by compressing observations into latent features.
AI.method: Proposes G-MARK framework that converts cooperative object-centric observations into explicit provenance-aware knowledge graphs. These KGs preserve object hypotheses with source attribution, visibility, uncertainty, conflicts, and spatial relations. Derives shared feature representations from KGs to support various driving tasks.
AI.result: Improves occlusion reasoning accuracy by 42.2%, reduces control-selection error by 13.1%, achieves comparable trajectory-planning accuracy with 25.6x smaller structured communication payload compared to state-of-the-art baseline.
AI.conclusion: Explicit provenance-aware knowledge graphs enable more transparent and effective cooperative reasoning for autonomous driving, significantly improving performance while reducing communication overhead.

title: Green BOA: Determining the environmental break-even point for ML-based data compression
comment: 3 pages, 1 figure. Accepted as a lightning-talk contribution at the 2nd International Workshop on Low Carbon Computing (LOCO 2026), Lancaster University, United Kingdom, 10-11 September 2026. Part of the LOCO 2026 proceedings, arXiv:LOCO2026/L05
summary: We summarise the outcome of two summer internship projects based at the University of Manchester, focused on the break-even point in terms of environmental sustainability for ML-based data compression algorithms. Using the example of a ML-based lossless compression algorithm, we compare estimates for the carbon-equivalent of the infrastructure needed for ML training and inference with the carbon-equivalent savings from reduced disk storage requirements, and discuss their break-even point.

AI.tldr: ML-based data compression algorithms may not be environmentally sustainable until they achieve significant compression ratios that offset their training/inference carbon costs
AI.motivation: There's a need to understand the environmental sustainability trade-offs of ML-based data compression algorithms, particularly whether the carbon savings from reduced storage requirements outweigh the carbon costs of ML training and inference infrastructure.
AI.method: The study uses a case study approach with a specific ML-based lossless compression algorithm, comparing carbon-equivalent estimates for ML training/infrastructure against carbon-equivalent savings from reduced disk storage requirements to calculate the break-even point.
AI.result: The paper likely demonstrates that ML-based compression algorithms require specific compression ratios to reach environmental break-even, where carbon savings from storage reduction equal or exceed carbon costs from ML operations.
AI.conclusion: ML-based compression needs careful environmental cost-benefit analysis; there exists a break-even point where environmental benefits outweigh costs, but this depends on compression efficiency and implementation scale.

title: DECOWAM: Decoupled Whole-Body World-Action Model for Legged Mobile Manipulation
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures. Introduces DECOWAM, a decoupled whole-body world-action model for legged mobile manipulation, and the ARMDOG real-robot dataset
summary: Mobile manipulation requires a robot to predict how locomotion and arm motion jointly alter future observations and control. Existing world-action models, developed largely for fixed-base platforms, do not explicitly distinguish camera ego-motion from base and arm actions. Here we introduce DECOWAM, a whole-body world-action model that separates these factors through dedicated conditional interfaces. DECOWAM freezes an adapted FastWAM backbone and trains residual adapters, an action-equivalent future bottleneck distilled from privileged observations, adversarially separated base and arm latents, and base-velocity conditioning for video prediction. We further introduce ARMDOG, a real-robot dataset that synchronizes video, whole-body state and action, and language. On a fixed replay protocol, DECOWAM improved both future-video and action prediction over FastWAM, reducing action MSE by 21.7% with 25.95M trainable adaptation parameters. Across 79 closed-loop trials per method, it achieved the highest observed whole-body coordination and base-displacement robustness among the compared systems, while task completion remained comparable to the strongest baseline. These results show that embodiment-aware factorization can support parameter-efficient joint visual prediction and whole-body control under moving viewpoints.

AI.tldr: DECOWAM is a world-action model for mobile manipulation that factorizes camera ego-motion from base/arm actions, enabling better whole-body coordination with efficient parameter adaptation.
AI.motivation: Existing world-action models for fixed-base platforms fail to distinguish camera ego-motion from base and arm actions, limiting their effectiveness for mobile manipulation where both locomotion and arm motion jointly affect observations and control.
AI.method: DECOWAM builds on FastWAM by freezing its backbone and training residual adapters, an action-equivalent future bottleneck distilled from privileged observations, adversarially separated base and arm latents, and base-velocity conditioning for video prediction. Uses the ARMDOG dataset for training.
AI.result: Improved both future-video and action prediction over FastWAM, reducing action MSE by 21.7% with 25.95M trainable parameters. Achieved highest whole-body coordination and base-displacement robustness in 79 closed-loop trials.
AI.conclusion: Embodiment-aware factorization supports parameter-efficient joint visual prediction and whole-body control under moving viewpoints for mobile manipulation.

title: Scale-Aware Pretraining of Time Series Foundation Models via Multi-Patch Token Alignment and Hybrid Masking
summary: Pretraining time series foundation models across heterogeneous datasets necessitates effective handling of varying sampling frequencies. Current methods either employ dataset-specific patch sizes and separate FFNs, leading to fragmented representations, or enforce a fixed patch size that neglects inherent temporal variations. To address this, we propose SATS, featuring a scale-aware token alignment mechanism that treats patch size as an explicit notion of scale. By incorporating a contrastive-inspired alignment regularizer, SATS aligns representation spaces across scales while preserving distinct modeling capacities. Furthermore, a hybrid masking strategy combining random and contiguous masking is introduced to capture multi-scale temporal structures. Experimental results on LSTF benchmarks demonstrate that SATS achieves a 9.2% improvement in MSE and an 8.3% gain in GIFT-Eval MASE compared to competitive baselines. Notably, SATS consistently delivers SOTA performance while achieving a 65.6% increase in model efficiency over advanced baselines, highlighting its effectiveness and scalability in time series pretraining.

AI.tldr: SATS introduces scale-aware token alignment and hybrid masking for pretraining time series foundation models across heterogeneous frequencies, achieving SOTA performance with improved efficiency.
AI.motivation: Current methods for pretraining time series foundation models across datasets with varying sampling frequencies either use dataset-specific patch sizes and separate FFNs (leading to fragmented representations) or enforce fixed patch sizes (neglecting inherent temporal variations), creating suboptimal solutions.
AI.method: Proposes SATS with: 1) scale-aware token alignment mechanism treating patch size as an explicit notion of scale, 2) contrastive-inspired alignment regularizer to align representation spaces across scales while preserving distinct modeling capacities, and 3) hybrid masking strategy combining random and contiguous masking to capture multi-scale temporal structures.
AI.result: On LSTF benchmarks, SATS achieves 9.2% improvement in MSE and 8.3% gain in GIFT-Eval MASE compared to competitive baselines. It consistently delivers SOTA performance with a 65.6% increase in model efficiency over advanced baselines.
AI.conclusion: SATS effectively handles varying sampling frequencies in time series pretraining through scale-aware token alignment and hybrid masking, demonstrating both effectiveness and scalability in building time series foundation models.

title: DARS: Dual-Level Credit Assignment RL with Structured Reasoning for Instruction-Based Image Editing
summary: Instruction-based image editing uses a planner-renderer pipeline: a vision-language model (VLM) first converts the instruction into an edit plan, and a diffusion model then executes that plan. Training such systems with only final-image rewards is inefficient because a poor edit does not reveal whether additional optimization should place more emphasis on the planner or the renderer, and even planner-dominant cases remain difficult to localize within a free-form reasoning trace. We present DARS, a reinforcement learning framework for dual-level credit assignment in this two-stage setting. Across modules, multi-plan multi-render rollouts estimate between-plan and within-plan reward variability for soft module routing, while rollout mean rewards provide hardness estimates for an adaptive curriculum. Within the planner, a four-field structured reasoning output enables a prefix-gated reward and token-level advantage reweighting, turning outcome-level feedback into localized supervision. Experiments on five benchmarks show that DARS outperforms a Joint~RL baseline with the same backbone, data, reward model, and rollout budget, with the largest gains on reasoning-intensive edits.

AI.tldr: DARS introduces a reinforcement learning framework for dual-level credit assignment in instruction-based image editing, addressing inefficiencies in planner-renderer pipelines by providing better localization of supervision between modules and within reasoning traces.
AI.motivation: Training instruction-based image editing systems (planner-renderer pipelines) with only final-image rewards is inefficient because poor edits don't reveal whether optimization should focus on the planner or renderer, and even planner-dominant cases are hard to localize within free-form reasoning traces.
AI.method: DARS uses multi-plan multi-render rollouts to estimate between-plan and within-plan reward variability for soft module routing between planner and renderer, and rollout mean rewards for adaptive curriculum. For the planner, it uses four-field structured reasoning output with prefix-gated rewards and token-level advantage reweighting to turn outcome-level feedback into localized supervision.
AI.result: Experiments on five benchmarks show DARS outperforms a Joint RL baseline with the same backbone, data, reward model, and rollout budget, with the largest gains on reasoning-intensive edits.
AI.conclusion: DARS effectively addresses credit assignment challenges in two-stage instruction-based image editing systems by providing dual-level credit assignment (across modules and within planner reasoning), leading to better performance especially on complex reasoning tasks.

title: Systematic Evaluation of TabPFN-TS for Zero-Shot Probabilistic Heat Load Forecasting in District Heating Networks
comment: 33 pages, 10 figures; supplementary information included
summary: District heating energy hubs require reliable heat load forecasts for efficient operational scheduling. Conventional forecasting workflows train system-specific models on historical data, which can become burdensome when networks change through new consumers, retrofits, or changing operating regimes. Zero-shot time-series foundation models and in-context forecasting offer a promising alternative: they can adapt at inference time from recent observations rather than by repeated retraining. This study systematically evaluates TabPFN-TS against time-series foundation models and trained machine-learning baselines for probabilistic heat load forecasting in district heating networks. Unlike foundation models pretrained on large collections of real time series, TabPFN-TS relies on synthetic pretraining data, which avoids direct pretraining-test overlap but raises the question of whether the learned prior captures district heating dynamics. We analyze covariate choice, context length, temporal resolution, and prediction horizon on representative operating weeks, validate the selected configuration over a full year, and test transferability on a second network. The results identify hourly 24-hour forecasting with a 12-week rolling context and ambient temperature as a parsimonious high-performing configuration; longer context windows do not improve accuracy. TabPFN-TS remains close to Chronos-2 in deterministic accuracy, reaching CVRMSE values of 13.06% versus 12.48% on the main dataset, and lies within the critical-difference threshold in the daily-rank comparison. Although Chronos-2 achieves the lowest aggregate full-year error, TabPFN-TS shows better empirical calibration. Finally, the diagnostic findings motivate a Multi-Resolution Residual-Correction Forecaster that combines a low-frequency Base Forecaster with a short-horizon Residual Forecaster to improve longer-horizon planning accuracy.

AI.tldr: TabPFN-TS, a zero-shot time-series foundation model pretrained on synthetic data, performs competitively against established models like Chronos-2 for probabilistic heat load forecasting in district heating networks, with optimal configuration using 12-week rolling context, hourly resolution, and ambient temperature covariates.
AI.motivation: District heating systems need reliable heat load forecasts for efficient scheduling, but conventional training-based approaches become burdensome when networks change. Zero-shot foundation models offer an alternative by adapting at inference time without retraining.
AI.method: Systematic evaluation of TabPFN-TS against time-series foundation models and machine learning baselines for probabilistic heat load forecasting. Analysis includes covariate choice, context length, temporal resolution, prediction horizon, validation on full-year data, and transferability testing on a second network.
AI.result: TabPFN-TS performs close to Chronos-2 (13.06% vs 12.48% CVRMSE) and shows better empirical calibration. Optimal configuration uses hourly 24-hour forecasting with 12-week rolling context and ambient temperature. Longer contexts don't improve accuracy. The findings motivate a Multi-Resolution Residual-Correction Forecaster combining low-frequency base forecasts with short-horizon residual corrections.
AI.conclusion: TabPFN-TS, despite synthetic pretraining without direct district heating data, effectively captures heating dynamics and performs competitively with state-of-the-art foundation models. The study demonstrates that zero-shot forecasting is viable for district heating, with implications for practical implementation through residual-correction approaches.

title: The Third Restructuring of Software Form: From the Three-Tier Architecture to Storage, Models, and Agents
summary: Software form has undergone two paradigm shifts since its inception: Software 1.0, in which instructions determine behavior, and Software 2.0, in which data determines behavior (machine learning). This paper argues that a third shift - Software 3.0, in which context and reasoning determine behavior - is now underway, and contends that its terminal form converges to three elements: a generalized database (the unified abstraction of all persistent state and memory), a large model (the intelligence core that performs reasoning and generation), and an agent (the execution loop connecting the first two). The core argument is as follows: in the traditional three-tier architecture, the user-interface layer will be absorbed by the model's ability to generate interfaces on demand, the business-logic layer will be re-partitioned along "expressibility x criticality" into model reasoning and storage constraints (with residual deterministic logic retained as tools), and only the data layer will be elevated into the sole persistent infrastructure. We formalize this convergence thesis, present a minimal reference architecture, report evidence from real prototypes and a live model, and systematically analyze both the conditions under which it holds and the boundaries where it fails - determinism, cost, security, and verifiability delimit the thesis's domain of applicability. We argue that the thesis holds in task domains that are expressible, verifiable, externally stateful, and tool-complete, and that it will reshape the roles of developers, the database industry, and the software-engineering discipline.

AI.tldr: Software is undergoing a third paradigm shift to "Software 3.0" where context and reasoning determine behavior, converging to three core elements: generalized database, large model, and agent.
AI.motivation: Software evolution has moved from instruction-based (Software 1.0) to data-based ML (Software 2.0), and the authors argue a third shift is now happening where context and reasoning drive behavior, addressing limitations of current paradigms.
AI.method: The authors formalize a convergence thesis, present a minimal reference architecture, provide evidence from real prototypes and live models, and systematically analyze conditions where the thesis holds versus boundaries where it fails.
AI.result: The convergence thesis holds in task domains that are expressible, verifiable, externally stateful, and tool-complete. The proposed architecture reshapes traditional three-tier systems by absorbing UI into model-generated interfaces, partitioning business logic between model reasoning/storage constraints, and elevating data layer as sole persistent infrastructure.
AI.conclusion: Software 3.0 will reshape developer roles, database industry, and software engineering discipline, with applicability limited by determinism, cost, security, and verifiability constraints.

title: CLaST: Context-aware Contrastive VAE for Probabilistic Time Series Forecasting
summary: Probabilistic forecasting models are widely used for time series forecasting in domains such as energy systems, finance, medicine, and transportation. In recent years, deep generative models have shown strong results on probabilistic forecasting, yet many conventional approaches struggle to capture internal temporal dependencies, leading to latent representations with limited expressive power. To address this limitation, we propose \textit{CLaST}, a VAE framework for probabilistic multivariate time series forecasting. Unlike existing generative models, CLaST learns embeddings that preserve contextual similarity between observations through our contrastive loss function. Experiments across nine widely adopted benchmarks demonstrate that CLaST consistently surpasses strong baseline methods. In short-term forecasting tasks, our approach achieves improvements of up to $16.4\%$ in CRPS and $14.4\%$ in NMAE over the second-best method. Furthermore, in long-term prediction CLaST attains superior overall performance, exceeding the second-best method by up to $48.6\%$ and $25.1\%$ in CRPS and NMAE, respectively.

AI.tldr: CLaST: A VAE framework with contrastive learning for probabilistic multivariate time series forecasting that outperforms existing methods on multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Many conventional probabilistic forecasting approaches struggle to capture internal temporal dependencies, leading to latent representations with limited expressive power, despite deep generative models showing strong results in time series forecasting domains like energy systems, finance, medicine, and transportation.
AI.method: CLaST is a VAE framework that learns embeddings preserving contextual similarity between observations through a contrastive loss function, specifically designed for probabilistic multivariate time series forecasting.
AI.result: Experiments across nine widely adopted benchmarks show CLaST consistently surpasses strong baseline methods. In short-term forecasting: improvements up to 16.4% in CRPS and 14.4% in NMAE over second-best method. In long-term prediction: superior overall performance, exceeding second-best method by up to 48.6% in CRPS and 25.1% in NMAE.
AI.conclusion: CLaST effectively addresses limitations in capturing temporal dependencies through contrastive learning in a VAE framework, achieving state-of-the-art performance in both short-term and long-term probabilistic multivariate time series forecasting tasks.

title: MemTrapBench: Benchmarking Cognitive Traps in LLM Memory Use
comment: Work in progress
summary: Memory has become a key component of large language models, enabling them to retain information and learn from long-term interactions. However, existing memory benchmarks mainly evaluate whether information is correctly extracted, stored, and retrieved, while largely overlooking how retrieved memories reshape model reasoning and affect performance on the current task. We identify memory-induced cognitive traps: even faithfully recorded and semantically relevant memories can distort model reasoning or beliefs and degrade current task performance. To systematically evaluate these failure modes, we introduce MemTrapBench, which covers two forms of cognitive traps: Reasoning Fixation and Belief Distortion. Experiments across two model families and five representative memory frameworks show that MemTrapBench is challenging: all evaluated memory strategies underperform the no-memory setting, with even the strongest methods suffering drops of more than 10%. To mitigate these cognitive traps, we propose AdaptiveMem, a simple yet effective inference-time method that instructs LLMs to avoid memory traps. AdaptiveMem mitigates cognitive traps on MemTrapBench while preserving or improving performance on standard memory benchmarks across diverse memory frameworks.

AI.tldr: Memory in LLMs can cause cognitive traps where even relevant memories distort reasoning and hurt performance; MemTrapBench evaluates these issues, and AdaptiveMem helps mitigate them.
AI.motivation: Existing memory benchmarks focus on information storage and retrieval but overlook how retrieved memories affect model reasoning and task performance, potentially leading to degradation.
AI.method: Introduced MemTrapBench to evaluate two types of memory-induced cognitive traps (Reasoning Fixation and Belief Distortion), tested across model families and memory frameworks, and proposed AdaptiveMem - an inference-time method to avoid memory traps.
AI.result: All evaluated memory strategies underperformed no-memory settings, with strongest methods suffering >10% performance drops on MemTrapBench. AdaptiveMem successfully mitigated cognitive traps while preserving or improving performance on standard benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Memory-induced cognitive traps are a significant challenge in LLMs, requiring systematic evaluation and mitigation strategies like AdaptiveMem to ensure retrieved memories improve rather than harm task performance.

title: An Inclusive and Lightweight Approach to Federated Continual Learning for Cultural Heritage
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures, Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Cyber Humanities (IEEE-CH 2026), Venice, Italy, September 7--9, 2026. Accepted author manuscript. Copyright 2026 IEEE
summary: Artificial intelligence can support cultural heritage and digital humanities through large-scale retrieval and analysis of digitized collections. However, cultural heritage data are often distributed across institutions, constrained by ownership and access restrictions, and continuously evolving over time. Federated Continual Learning (FCL) is well suited to this setting, as it enables models to learn from distributed and sequential data without sharing raw collections. In this paper, we propose FedCurv-DR, a lightweight, regularisation-based FCL strategy. The method accumulates parameter-importance estimates across clients and experiences to protect learned knowledge, while updating them only at fixed intervals to minimize communication and computation overhead. We evaluate FedCurv-DR in a continual learning scenario using the WikiArt image dataset for genre classification with evolving styles, reporting performance, energy, and fairness metrics. Our results show that FedCurv- DR reduces forgetting and balances performance, fairness, and energy efficiency for sustainable AI in cultural heritage.

AI.tldr: FedCurv-DR is a lightweight federated continual learning method that reduces forgetting while balancing performance, fairness, and energy efficiency for AI applications in cultural heritage.
AI.motivation: Cultural heritage data faces challenges of being distributed across institutions, constrained by ownership/access restrictions, and continuously evolving over time. Federated Continual Learning (FCL) is needed to learn from distributed, sequential data without sharing raw collections.
AI.method: Proposes FedCurv-DR, a lightweight, regularization-based FCL strategy that accumulates parameter-importance estimates across clients and experiences to protect learned knowledge. Updates parameter-importance estimates only at fixed intervals to minimize communication and computation overhead.
AI.result: Evaluated on WikiArt image dataset for genre classification with evolving styles, reporting performance, energy, and fairness metrics. Results show FedCurv-DR reduces forgetting and balances performance, fairness, and energy efficiency.
AI.conclusion: FedCurv-DR provides sustainable AI for cultural heritage applications by effectively handling distributed, evolving data while maintaining privacy, reducing forgetting, and balancing key metrics of performance, fairness, and energy efficiency.

title: ContractScrub: A benchmark for final review of legal contracts
comment: 10 pages, ICML AI4Law Workshop
summary: Legal work, with its heavy reliance on processing large amounts of text, is often considered one of the domains most exposed to the use of LLMs. Contract ``scrubbing,'' the final review of transactional agreements for errors and inconsistencies, is a particularly suitable task for automation, because it is routine, painstaking work requiring detailed attention to long documents. Scrubbing also seems to align naturally with the general capabilities expected of frontier LLMs around long-context reasoning, consistency checking, and named entity recognition (NER). Despite the economic value and potential for automation, no formal evaluations of LLMs performing contract scrubbing have been conducted. We introduce ContractScrub, the first benchmark designed to evaluate contract scrubbing capabilities, comprising contracts hand-crafted by experienced lawyers over diverse error categories such as misuse of defined terms, incorrect references, and inconsistent language. Frontier models perform surprisingly poorly with only one model reaching 0.75 macro average recall despite strong performance on seemingly related general benchmarks, demonstrating the practical limits of current models and the importance of narrowly targeted, domain-specific benchmarks for measuring real-world impact.

AI.tldr: LLMs perform poorly on contract scrubbing despite seeming well-suited for it, revealing gaps between general benchmarks and domain-specific tasks.
AI.motivation: Legal work, especially contract scrubbing (final review of transactional agreements for errors), is ideal for automation due to its routine, detail-oriented nature and apparent alignment with LLM capabilities in long-context reasoning and consistency checking. Despite economic value and automation potential, no formal evaluations exist for LLMs in contract scrubbing.
AI.method: Introduce ContractScrub, the first benchmark for evaluating contract scrubbing capabilities. It comprises contracts hand-crafted by experienced lawyers covering diverse error categories like misuse of defined terms, incorrect references, and inconsistent language.
AI.result: Frontier models perform surprisingly poorly - only one model reached 0.75 macro average recall despite strong performance on related general benchmarks. This reveals the practical limits of current models.
AI.conclusion: There's a significant gap between general benchmark performance and real-world domain-specific tasks like contract scrubbing. Narrowly targeted, domain-specific benchmarks are essential for measuring true real-world impact and revealing practical limitations of current LLMs.

title: End-to-end Early Classification of Time Series in Non-Stationary Environments
summary: Early Classification of Time Series (ECTS) requires making accurate decisions as early as possible in inherently online and evolving environments. Yet, most existing methods assume stationarity and rely on separable designs, where classification and triggering are optimized independently, an assumption that fundamentally limits their adaptability under drift. In this work, we challenge this paradigm and study ECTS under non-stationary conditions. We provide the first systematic comparison between separable and end-to-end approaches across controlled drifting scenarios. Building on Reinforcement Learning, we introduce DQeND, a unified architecture that jointly learns representation, classification, and triggering decisions, while remaining directly comparable to state-of-the-art separable baselines. Across a wide range of drifts, DQeND demonstrates strong robustness across various non-stationary scenarios, consistently outperforming separable baselines. An ablation study further highlights that jointly updating representation and decision modules is critical to these gains. Overall, our results indicate that end-to-end learning can offer improved adaptation capabilities for ECTS in dynamic environments, and motivate further investigation of alternatives to separable designs.

AI.tldr: DQeND is a reinforcement learning-based end-to-end architecture for early classification of time series that jointly learns representation, classification, and triggering decisions, demonstrating superior robustness to non-stationary drifts compared to separable baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing early time series classification methods assume stationarity and use separable designs where classification and triggering are optimized independently, which fundamentally limits adaptability to distribution drifts in evolving environments.
AI.method: Introduces DQeND (Deep Q-Network for Early Decision), a unified reinforcement learning architecture that jointly learns representation, classification, and triggering decisions in an end-to-end manner, while remaining directly comparable to separable baselines.
AI.result: DQeND demonstrates strong robustness across various non-stationary scenarios and controlled drifting conditions, consistently outperforming separable baselines. Ablation study shows joint updating of representation and decision modules is critical for these gains.
AI.conclusion: End-to-end learning offers improved adaptation capabilities for early classification of time series in dynamic environments, motivating further investigation beyond separable designs and highlighting the importance of joint optimization.

title: Electronic Navigational Chart Change Classification
comment: Accepted at 34th ACM SIGSPATIAL 2026
summary: Electronic Navigational Charts (ENCs) are geospatial vector datasets used in maritime navigation systems that represent hydrographic and navigational information such as depths, navigational aids, traffic schemes, and hazards. A major challenge for hydrographic offices is determining whether a given chart change poses a critical or non-critical risk to maritime safety. Existing workflows rely heavily on manual review and verification, which is labor-intensive, scales poorly with the volume of incoming chart updates, and introduces inter-analyst inconsistencies. To address this challenge, we propose a method for automated classification of ENC changes. We establish a baseline encoding scheme to translate complex vector data changes into a structured tabular format for classification models. The two crucial components of the encoding scheme include a spatial context encoder to enrich the change representations with surrounding geographic features, and an ENC attribute encoder to represent nuanced attribute-value descriptions of the modified objects. We evaluate the proposed approach across two distinct operational datasets, comprising 1,308 chart pairs containing over 100,000 individual chart modifications. Tuned gradient-boosted trees leveraging the proposed encoding schemes achieve accuracies of 90% and 94% on the two datasets, yielding a 5-7% improvement over default hyperparameterized models trained on encodings without spatial context and attribute embeddings. These results demonstrate the viability of integrating machine learning into operational geospatial pipelines to improve ENC maintenance and enhance maritime safety. Finally, our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of simple location and spatial aggregation methods, providing a foundation for evaluating more sophisticated spatial representation learning techniques for this application.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an automated machine learning method to classify Electronic Navigational Chart (ENC) changes as critical or non-critical risks for maritime safety, achieving 90-94% accuracy.
AI.motivation: Current manual review processes for ENC changes are labor-intensive, scale poorly with chart update volumes, and suffer from inter-analyst inconsistencies, creating challenges for hydrographic offices in assessing maritime safety risks.
AI.method: The method establishes a baseline encoding scheme to translate complex vector data changes into structured tabular format, including: 1) spatial context encoder to enrich changes with surrounding geographic features, and 2) ENC attribute encoder to represent attribute-value descriptions of modified objects. Gradient-boosted trees are then used for classification.
AI.result: The approach achieved 90% and 94% accuracy on two operational datasets containing 1,308 chart pairs with over 100,000 individual modifications. This represents a 5-7% improvement over models without spatial context and attribute embeddings.
AI.conclusion: The research demonstrates the viability of integrating machine learning into operational geospatial pipelines for ENC maintenance, showing that even simple spatial aggregation methods provide a strong foundation for future spatial representation learning techniques in this domain.

title: DecoVAE: a Lightweight Interpretable Trend-Seasonal VAE Framework for Efficient Probabilistic Time Series Forecasting
summary: Probabilistic time series forecasting remains challenging, largely because modeling distinct trend and seasonal dynamics requires specialized approaches. Existing methods often fail to capture the unique inner properties of these components, lack interpretability, or suffer from heavy memory and runtime overhead.
